Foreword You are holding the yearbook of the Royal Netherlands Navy 2016. In this annual overview, you will read about how the navy was deployed in major international operations and exercises, and what happened on shore to make all of this possible. Prominent in 2016 was the provision of emergency assistance. After the devastating force of Hurricane Matthew, particularly Haiti lay in ruins and there were significant shortages of basic necessities. Various ships set course for the affected country to provide aid and deliver supplies. Marines were also deployed to ensure that the assistance could be distributed safely among the population. Additionally, the navy also showcased its best side in the Mediterranean by rescuing migrants in perilous situations at sea. The maintenance program for the Walrus-class submarines is well underway, and the maintenance of Zr.Ms. Van Speijk was successfully completed. Personnel underwent many new trainings, courses, and participated in (international) exercises. During the World Port Days in Rotterdam, the navy was present with marines and several ships to introduce visitors to our work. We hope that this Yearbook will prove to be a useful reference work. 18 19 Organizational Overviews Organizational Overviews Department of Finance and Control (F&C) Head: Captain (ktz) M.F.C.M. Spierings The tasks of the F&C department consist of supporting C-ZSK by providing preparation, execution, progress, and quality of financial policy advice. Additionally, compiling the budget, establishing the expenditure program, executing financial management, as well as contributing to information provision through management and steering reports, are part of the responsibilities. Finally, the department prepares the cash forecast quarterly, which also includes proposed measures to remain within the financial frameworks. The expenditures by C-ZSK (Article 2 of the defense budget) were higher than budgeted last year. This increase was largely caused by personnel expenditures and additional costs for readiness and maintenance. Furthermore, C-ZSK deployment, partly as a result of the involvement with the European Border and Coast Guard Agency Frontex and the European Union Naval Force Mediterranean, better known as EU Operation Sophia, accounted for a larger share of the BIV budget (Article 1, defense budget) this year. In response to the increasing pressure on the defense budget, an Interdepartmental Policy Investigation (IBO) was conducted this year into the readiness process. This particularly mapped and analyzed the costs of deployment and readiness of the amphibious transport ships (LPDs). It became clear that the extensive deployment was displacing the available resources for readiness for basic warfare tasks. Additionally, a significant portion of the costs incurred for deployment was not reimbursed through the BIV. The financial challenges this year were further exacerbated by a rising necessity to replace outdated systems or repair them more frequently due to delays in replacement investments. Furthermore, the available budget limited the possibilities to maintain logistical supplies, resulting in an increasing so-called logistical debt. This year, the study 'Policy Review Marine Study' was also published. The starting point for this was the namesake study from 2005, based on which the composition of the fleet changed drastically. The study revealed that despite the fact that not all investment plans had been realized, all financial expenditures and the subsequent decision-making proceeded in a controlled manner. Thus, there was no need for additional measures. Zr.Ms. Rotterdam facilitates the training of the local coast guard near Libya by British and German instructors, by providing hospitality on board with accommodation, meals, and prayer spaces.

This judgment primarily stemmed from the conducted partial study by the Audit Service of the State (ADR), attached to the report as an appendix. The most significant conclusion stated that due to the changed security situation since 2014, one of the three premises of the Navy Study had become outdated, making a new reflection on the composition of the fleet seem unavoidable. In the Caribbean, preparations have been completed to formally transfer the temporary payment office CARIB, currently under the director controller of the Commander of the Naval Forces Caribbean Area (CMZCARIB), to the Financial Administration and Management Office (FABK) as part of the FABK reorganization, effective 2017. To have more guidance in determining the appropriate stance of the controller in the current organizational structure, the Directorate of Finance and Control (HDFC) issued a guideline on 'control'. This guideline prescribes, among other things, how the controller can best act as a critical sparring partner for line organizations through provocative questions. Early involvement in decision-making, a good information position, and an actively validating attitude are of great importance. This role was further defined through a thorough revision of the CZSK standard framework. SAP enabled improved cost insight. As a result, it became increasingly possible to standardize the 'budgeting process'. This means that relationships between objectives, activities, and expenditures are made more visible based on standards, thereby creating better steering possibilities. Loos-Gelijns The Directorate of Personnel and Operations (DPBV) is the supporting directorate within CZSK and the Coast Guard in the areas of personnel, training, healthcare, organization, operations, and information provision. Additionally, the directorate serves as an important link to the Defense Staff/Administrative Staff through the Integration department. For 2015, the focal points of the directorate were: 1. Optimizing operations in the broadest sense of the word. An important step has been taken in establishing a new business plan, which will be further developed in the coming years. Simplified organizational chart of the Directorate of Personnel and Operations (DPBV).

22 23 Directorate of Personnel and Operations Directorate of Personnel and Operations 2. Ensure that the personnel structure of CZSK is fully staffed in 2020, with a target of 98% in permanent positions and 2% flexible deployment consisting of reservists and hired personnel. To achieve this, the P-continuity project started in 2015. 3. Further professionalization of personnel management and care within CZSK. This involved matters such as Professionally Oriented Training (BGO), employability, leadership development, and ensuring integrated healthcare. 4. Intensifying cooperation between (internal) Defense, regional civil (in training), and international partners. 5. Intensifying the management role of CZSK for the Coast Guard Netherlands and CARIB, with special attention to long-term sustainability. 6. Further developing the adaptability of the CZSK organization to changing circumstances, both within Defense and in society. This was particularly relevant for the supporting and administrative processes. In practice, this proved to be considerably more challenging, but the organization must be sufficiently prepared for the future, and therefore it is deemed necessary for this process to continue. Personnel and Organization The further elaboration of the first partial agreement was still pending in 2016, which hindered the job allocation process due to uncertainty about when a new service end system would be implemented. At the end of November, an interim arrangement was put into effect, allowing personnel with a retirement date in 2017 to choose to work longer for a period of up to two years, until the new system is implemented. Due to increasing personnel shortages and a high ambition level of the organization, it became increasingly difficult in 2016 to find suitable solutions for personnel issues and vacancies. By clearly prioritizing and, where necessary, holding even more intensive consultations with the relevant departments and units, suitable solutions were found. The task assignment of the respective unit was also regularly adjusted. Following the vision document prepared by the Defense Personnel & Organization Division (DPOD) regarding the further development of the HR functions within the organization, a Cougar helicopter conducts fast rope training with marines.

24 25 Directorate of Personnel and Operations Directorate of Personnel and Operations Defense, a number of advisors from HR together with colleagues from other branches of the armed forces have considered the challenges faced by HR professionals in 2020. Based on their proposals, this will continue in 2017, focusing on strategic HR themes such as talent management, strategic workforce planning, further development of the HRM system (E-HRM), sustainable employability, the change agent, and the driver of social innovation. Career Guidance Career guidance involves aligning the wishes of personnel with the opportunities provided by the organization. This alignment takes place in the form of a career conversation, which is held during each position or once every three years. This conversation focuses on personal developments in the near future and in the (medium) long term. The personal development of the employee is necessary to remain valuable to the organization. In addition to this internal mobility, the career counselor also pays attention to external mobility for employees who will not advance in the long term but will leave Defense. The career guidance section consists of four military offices for the operational service groups, marines, technical service, logistics service, and one office for civilian personnel. At the beginning of 2016, this section had 37 military positions and 1 civilian position, of which a total of two were temporary positions. During the past year, one temporary position at the Marine Career Guidance Office and Technical Service was made permanent in the formation. Additionally, during the course of this year, a second civilian career counselor for civilian personnel was appointed. These three new permanent positions are funded from the Motie-Van der Staaij (MvdS) funds. Various groups of personnel, such as junior officers and the middle management among non-commissioned officers, experienced shortages. Unlike the previous year, a decision was made to implement more differentiation in compensation. In 2016, the 'Technical Allowance' was introduced for the next three years, which means that technical personnel in the rank of corporal up to and including warrant officer will receive a retention bonus under certain conditions. The idea behind this is that a retention bonus over multiple years will have more effect than the usual one or two years. Furthermore, an excessive number of first lieutenants of marines and corporals of technical service should eventually fill the shortages in the next higher ranks. Another sub-project within P-continuity that took shape is the establishment of Subject Matter Experts for various career paths. Questionnaires were also compiled to collect data on irregular departures and dropouts in initial training. HR made every effort to contribute maximally to "Safety at and from the sea," by placing the right people with the right training in the right positions. Integration The Integration department consists of the offices of Strategy & Advice (S&A), Policy Planning & Budgeting (BPB), and Investments (INV). Office of Strategy & Advice The S&A Office supports the Commander of the Naval Forces (C-ZSK) in his role as maritime military advisor to the Commander of the Armed Forces and the Minister of Defense. In 2016, the decision was made to work within S&A in three teams: Policy team, Knowledge team, and International Military Cooperation (IMS) team. The Directorate of Materiel Maintenance (DMI) provides for the periodic and major maintenance of all vessels of the Royal Netherlands Navy. Here is a submarine of the Walrus class.

30 31 Directorate of Personnel and Operations Directorate of Personnel and Operations detachment present on the Greek island of Chios as part of FRONTEX. In preparation for this, considerations were made regarding the provision of good personnel care, including aftercare. Additionally, the FRISC (Fast Response Intervention Ship Command) operators received a brief supplementary medical training on dealing with drowning victims and hypothermia. In March, Zr.Ms. Van Amstel departed for the Aegean Sea as part of Standing NATO Maritime Group 2 (SNMG2). At that time, there were still significant migrant flows between Turkey and Greece, and there was a possibility of having to rescue drowning victims in the event of a SOLAS case, so a plan was developed in preparation for how to accommodate the migrants. This took into account medical aspects such as extra oxygen, medication, and a reception plan. There was considerable attention to the aspects of Hygiene Preventive Medicine (HPG). Infectious diseases, such as scabies and lice, are present among migrants, and good HPG measures could prevent this from being transmitted to the crew. An additional AMV (Medical Assistant) was also added to increase medical capacity. During its deployment in the Aegean Sea, the Van Amstel did not have to rescue any drowning victims. At the beginning of May, it became clear that the Van Amstel would also be deployed as part of FRONTEX in the Mediterranean Sea between Italy and Libya. Experiences from other ships in this area indicated that migrants often needed to be rescued from unseaworthy vessels. Reports from allied nations showed that there were many minors and pregnant women among the migrants. In preparation for FRONTEX, the reception plan for migrants was reviewed in detail regarding HPG and medical aspects. Given the potentially large number of migrants to be accommodated over 24 to 48 hours, the medical team was expanded to a total of two AMA (Medical Officers) and three AMV (Medical Assistants). Additional courses and internships in pediatrics and obstetrics were undertaken in preparation. A total of 1,057 migrants were accommodated. However, on June 16, a baby named Gelila was born on board the Van Amstel under the supervision of the medical team, bringing the total number of migrants to 1,058. From October 19 to November 26, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam was deployed in the Mediterranean Sea as part of Operation Sophia. Libyan coast guard personnel who were also on board were trained during this deployment. Additionally, necessary preparations regarding HPG took place again before the deployment, and the medical team was once again expanded. During this deployment, no migrants were accommodated. The crew of Zr.Ms. Van Amstel cares for migrants during Operation FRONTEX.

28 29 Directorate of Personnel and Operations Directorate of Personnel and Operations Operations and Information Provision Head: Captain (ktz) R. de Korte The year 2016 presented a significant number of challenges for the Operations & Information Provision (BVIV) department. Both the IT landscape and operational management were in full swing. Following the approval obtained in 2015, the department began establishing the ERP Competence Center CZSK (EC3). This required reviewing job descriptions and subsequently going through recruitment processes. By December 31, 2016, the EC3 was ready and was eighty percent staffed. The department also began taking over activities from the Sea Chain program (responsible for the CZSK migration to SAP), which ended on July 1. The program started with the takeover of the U2SAP project, which is responsible for the migration of material logistics operations from ULTIMO to SAP. U2SAP proved to be a complex project in 2016 that required significant attention from both BVIV and the users. Part of the project was completed this year, while the remaining portion is to be completed in 2017. The projects Migration Mercuur and Karel Doorman also took place under the auspices of BVIV in 2016 and were completed. Additionally, BVIV took over the documentation and temporary personnel, including contracted staff, from the Sea Chain program. The management that the department exercises over the phasing out of legacy IT systems, whose functionalities are being taken over by ERP M&F, remains essential. By the end of the year, the dismantling of a cluster of these legacy IT systems, which have influenced the material logistics operations of the Royal Netherlands Navy for many years (such as VAS, SGA, VPA, BUVA, BBSKM, FIDOKM, MATRACS, POS), was completed. This allows the department to gain further experience with the challenges surrounding the phasing out of applications. This is necessary as the phasing out or rationalization of applications is receiving increasing attention within Defense. The impetus for this is the intended transition of Defense to a new IT that is better able to support future IT-supported operations and command management. Not only is the migration to the new IT facilitated when there are fewer applications; where possible, savings on operating costs also follow. This phasing out certainly impacts the CZSK. In 2016, the Defense-wide program Border-Extending IT (GrIT) was initiated, which is to ensure the new IT in the coming years. The above also influenced the interface that BVIV forms between the Defense IT provider, the Joint IV Command (JIVC), and the Executive Staff, where the IT budgets are allocated. A new method of managing IT activities was introduced from the Executive Staff, the project portfolio management (PPM). The department participated in this PPM and coordinated the CZSK interests in an overstretched IT landscape where capacity, knowledge, and expertise in IT are scarce. The needs statement for E-welfare (internet) on board ships, established in 2015, will be honored for 2017. The department began planning activities to implement this project. A pilot was also initiated to improve internet provision at the barracks in Den Helder. Additionally, in 2016, E-welfare (internet) was delivered for the Marine Corps. Medical and Personnel Care Medical Care Operational Medicine Medcell 2016 was a varied and changeable operational year. There were many changes regarding planned ships and types of deployment concerning the Operational Year Plan (OJP). Notably, there were missions in the Mediterranean related to the migrant flows to Europe. From January 2016, there was a Fast Raiding Interception & Special Forces Craft (FRISC). During the training of members of the Libyan Coast Guard by British and German forces, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam served as the 'mother ship'.

32 33 Directorate of Personnel and Operations Directorate of Personnel and Operations In the second half of 2016, Zr.Ms. De Ruyter was deployed as the flagship of SNMG2 in the Aegean Sea with a German staff. During this period, the flow of migrants between Turkey and Greece decreased significantly; therefore, there was no expansion of the medical team. The LCF De Ruyter rescued two drowning individuals who were attempting to swim from Turkey to Greece. After several hours under medical observation, they were handed over to the Turkish coast guard. The ship's doctor was also the Medical Advisor (MEDAD) for the German staff. From August to December, Zr.Ms. Tromp was deployed as the flagship for the anti-piracy mission Atalanta near the Horn of Africa. The naval vessel was augmented with an Advanced Resuscitation Team (ART) for this purpose. Due to the duration of the deployment, three rotations of surgical teams from the IDR took place. The ship's doctor on the Tromp was also the MEDAD for the staff. The deployment of a 'West ship' remained unchanged. In January, Zr.Ms. Friesland returned from the West, after which Zr.Ms. De Zeven Provinciën, Zr.Ms. Groningen, and Zr.Ms. Holland departed for the West. The Holland, together with Zr.Ms. Pelikaan, was deployed for emergency aid following a hurricane in Haiti. The Holland conducted many beach landings to distribute water and food supplies but did not provide medical support. From the Pelikaan, limited medical emergency assistance was provided in remote areas. Throughout the year, medical support was provided to the Vessel Protection Detachments (VPD) of the Marine Corps in the Indian Ocean by adding a Medical Assistant (AMV-er) to each VPD team. During the year, an ATG was on standby, including a Role 2 Afloat for 20 days NTM. The personnel for this were ready, and most of the equipment was also available. However, there was no budget to purchase the remaining materials. On Zr.Ms. Van Amstel, a crew member distracts a young migrant with a stuffed animal. A German Orion conducts a practice airdrop in the Indian Ocean alongside Zr.Ms. Tromp. The container dropped by parachute is recovered by the Nautical Service.

26 27 Directorate of Personnel and Operations Directorate of Personnel and Operations Policy acts as the first point of contact (mailbox) for the Defense Staff and the Executive Staff (Main Directorates) regarding policy documents, studies, parliamentary matters, and the so-called Hague consultations. Important activities this year included efforts within the framework of the 'Development of the Armed Forces' (DOKM) concerning the strengthening and renewal of the armed forces. The Knowledge team delved into the 'new' domains of Hybrid Warfare, Cyber, and Space in 2016 and contributed to various follow-up assignments under DOKM, such as 'Information as a Weapon' and 'Information as an Enabler'. This team was also actively involved in the network of the foundation 'Netherlands Maritime Country' and the analysis of the inspection reports from the Inspector General of the Armed Forces regarding visits to CZSK units. The IMS team supports CZSK in its international contacts and collaborations in cooperation with the Defense Staff (IMS). In addition to preparations for regular meetings within the framework of Belgian-Dutch cooperation (BeNeSaM) and the Naval Steering Group (NSG) with Germany, a highlight in 2016 was the organization of the Channel Command (CHANCOM) meeting. The Policy Planning & Budgeting Office (BPB) The Planning Coordination & Integration section (PLINT) is responsible for the integral planning process within CZSK. Over the past year, PLINT, in close cooperation with Finance & Control (F&C), proposed integral measures to Consumer Products and Retail (CP&R) and All Risks (AR) to keep the realization in 2016 within the budgetary framework. Mid-year discussions were also held with the Executive Staff regarding this. As a result, the execution this year was managed. In drafting the business plan for 2017, the integral planning was further improved. The Group Leaders and CP&R were explicitly involved for the first time in determining the key multi-year objectives to be achieved and the necessary activities for that. The increased focus on the groups contributes to more product-oriented thinking and working within CZSK operations. The implementation of the MvdS measures was already in full swing, and the first personnel arrived in 2016. Regarding equipment, the additional MvdS budget was partly spent on re-supply. The desk note was replaced this year as input from the DOs in the Bureau Policy, Planning & Budgeting (BPB) process by the execution note. As a result of the internal planning process, issues such as logistical debt, obsolescence problems, and currency issues were raised. The additional funds for enhancing operational readiness in the 2017 budget will be used to address issues from the 2016 desk note. As part of the BPB office, the Programming section is responsible for the establishment of the Readiness Plan (GSP). This GSP forms the long-term plan of the CZSK and looks about ten years ahead. It serves as the basis for various sub-plans within the CZSK, including the Maintenance Plan of the DMI, the Operational Annual Plan of the DOPS, the filling plan of P&O, and the training plan of Royal Netherlands Navy Training (OKM). This year, the establishment proved to be a dynamic process, where all parties involved had to regularly adapt flexibly to rapidly changing environmental factors affecting both the GSP and the various sub-plans. Changes in the Maintenance Program for the Walrus class (IPW) are an example of this. Furthermore, 2016 was focused on creating 'contingency plans' in preparation for expected financial shortfalls. For the Mine (Counter Measures Vessels) Operational Sea Training (M(CMV)OST) section, 2016 was marked by the responsibility for planning and monitoring material exploitation, particularly in the context of further implementing the demand and supply management (VAM) organization and processes. Additionally, under the leadership of CDS/DAOG, work was done on drafting the Defense Exploitation Plan – Weapon Systems (DEP-W). Of course, there were also several material processes that required the 'magic oil' of the section. As a result of MvdS, the section was expanded at the end of the year with a new component that must coordinate the introduction of new or renewed equipment within CZSK. The Investment Bureau (INV) is responsible within CZSK for the planning and realization of the bandwidth budget allocated to the defense components from the Defense Investment Plan (DIP). The Netherlands Maritime Force (NLMARFOR) consists of three staffs: the (operationally deployable) Maritime Battle Staff (MBS) and the two training staffs Marine Training Command (MTC) and Sea Train Command (STC).

Maritime Battle Staff (MBS) 
Commander: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) L.G.J. van den Berg, succeeded by Captain (ktz) F.J.G. Lenssen 

The Maritime Battle Staff (MBS) is the deployable C2 element of NLMARFOR. The MBS has various forms of appearance. In order of complexity, these are Commander Amphibious Task Group (CATG), Commander Task Group/Commander Task Force (CTG/CTF), and specific staff elements such as Mine Counter Measures – Tasking Authority (MCM-TA). As CATG, the MBS must be deployable within a readiness period of seven to – depending on the chosen organization – twenty days. In some cases, the MBS must be supplemented for deployment as CATG with pre-identified and (partially) trained personnel from the CZSK and other operational commands (OPCOs) (augmentees). 

The main task of the MBS is to plan, coordinate, prepare, and execute (inter)national joint exercises and operations in which single deployed units (operationally ready naval and/or marine units) operate together to maintain operational readiness. 

In 2016, the MBS was active in various forms, during which the following diverse exercises were conducted:

COLD RESPONSE (February 18 to March 16) 
Participation in Cold Response was for NLMARFOR focused on maintaining the amphibious capabilities of MBS during the NRF year. Exercises were conducted in the highest spectrum of violence under the most extreme winter conditions. COMNLMARFOR led an amphibious task group consisting of Dutch, British, and American marines, Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam, USS Fort McHenry, and two Cougar helicopters. During Cold Response, a CET-FIT period was conducted in the vicinity of Harstad, Norway, where participating units followed a fixed program to increase interoperability. During the tactical phase, two landings were executed at Namsos. Close cooperation was maintained with SNMG1 and Norwegian units to protect the Amphibious Task Group (ATG) during the preparation and execution of the landings.

TRUTHFUL SWORD (April 11 to 22) 
Truthful Sword 16 was a Command Post Exercise (CPX) that took place in Wildflecken, Germany. The exercise was the first milestone in the certification of 1 German/Netherlands Marine.

70 71 Directorate Operations Directorate Operations EMERALD MOVE (September 21 to October 14) Near the Italian island of Sardinia, MBS participated in the exercise Emerald Move. A total of ten European countries, including France, Spain, and Great Britain, practiced for the European Amphibious Initiative. The aim of this initiative is to create a multinational amphibious unit that can be deployed anywhere, both in EU and NATO operations. This year, the exercise was led by Italy and focused on testing and improving cooperation between the different nationalities. The Dutch participation consisted of Zr.Ms. Rotterdam, which had 117 marines on board for this purpose. The program included many different exercises and a so-called freeplay phase in which air strikes, submarine threats, and amphibious landings were practiced. A small team from MBS participated in the planning and execution of this exercise. This included the deployment phase in the early stage of a small joint land-heavy operation for the subsequent certification exercise Trident Jaguar 17. For 1GNC, NLMARFOR is the natural partner in the maritime domain to operate (bi-) nationally at Joint Task Force level. During the execution of the exercise at the NATO Joint Forces Training Centre (JFTC) in Bydgoszcz, Poland, the MBS team acted as Maritime Component Command (MCC) and as a maritime advisor within the Initial Command Element (ICE). The team demonstrated the potential of maritime and amphibious capabilities to support a land operation and also emphasized the importance of cooperation with commercial shipping through the Naval Cooperation and Guidance for Shipping (NCAGS) organization. NATO Response Force (NRF) COMNLMARFOR was responsible as Commander Amphibious Task Group (CATG) for forming and preparing the Dutch Amphibious Task Group (ATG) as part of the CZSK contribution to the NRF for 2016. Throughout the year, the ATG was on 20 days notice-to-move. This year was designated as the standby year. The composition of the ATG varied each month. The maritime contribution consisted of one or more amphibious transport ships, a submarine, a mine countermeasure vessel, a LCF, an M-frigate, and a hydrographic survey vessel. The core of the landing force was formed by 2MCG, C-battery with 120mm mortars from the VUSTCO, a TL platoon with the weapon system Stinger from DGLC, and enablers from (M)EODD, CMI, VSW, MEIC, and a cyber element. The ATG was capable of being deployed anywhere in the world as part of NRF16 within the entire spectrum of violence, for a continuous period of 30 days, within 20 days. The higher command (1-up) was fulfilled by UKMARFOR, which took on the role of MCC. The ATG was not activated during the standby year. The next ATG contribution as part of NRF is scheduled for 2020. Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt Commander: cdt R.T. Luyckx, from June 16 kltz R. van Twuijver, from July 18 acting commander/executive officer kltz J. Veken During the first half of 2016, Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt formed the amphibious task group of the NATO Response Force (NRF) together with other fleet and marine units, Special Operations Forces, and the NLMARFOR-Maritime Battle Staff. The NRF is on standby to respond quickly in case of conflicts or to provide humanitarian assistance. To ensure the amphibious operational capabilities for the NRF, Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt participated in two major amphibious exercise scenarios during that period, namely Cold Response and BALTOPS. Cold Response began a decade ago as a peacekeeping/peace enforcing exercise but is increasingly taking on characteristics of a classic 'steel-on-steel training'. This is mainly due to the tense relationship with Russia. Amphibious warfare, or combat at the boundary of land and water, is one of the priorities of the Dutch navy and our NATO allies. It was therefore not surprising that between February 19 and March 5, dots appeared on the horizon between the fjords off the Norwegian coast. Upon approach, it became clear that it concerned Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam, and the American USS Fort McHenry. Both small vessels, manned by American, British, and Dutch marines, as well as various helicopters filled with sea soldiers, took off from the warships to participate in this exercise. From both the air and the water, about 350 marines, equipped with mortars among other things, landed. They advanced towards the nearby Namsos to secure two strategically important bridges so that ground troops could push through. There was some enemy resistance, but the marines, with the help of air support from four Norwegian F-16s, maintained control and drove the opponent away. Thus, the mission of the amphibious task group was successful. During the BALTOPS exercise (June 6 to 16), the amphibious training opportunities in a multinational setting were extensively utilized. Together with the British HMS Ocean and the American USS Carter Hall, the Dutch LPD was assigned to an amphibious task group under American leadership. Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt had a Swedish-Finnish task group on board for the occasion, the Swedish-Finnish Amphibious Task Unit (SFATU). The Swedish battalion staff was supplemented with Finnish staff officers and a complete Finnish company. Additionally, a German platoon was accommodated in this company, which was a guest on board Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt, as part of the cooperation between the Marine Corps and the German Seebataillon. From Sweden, five Combat Boats (CB90) were also embarked that were part of the SFATU. Furthermore, several Finnish vessels (Jurmo and Jehu) joined this boat group in the theater. Finally, the Netherlands added two Cougar helicopters from the Defense Helicopter Command to the exercise. May 24, Girls' Day on Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt.

Zr.Ms. Groningen Commander: kltz W.A. Hansen, from March 11 kltz H.M. Sinke Zr.Ms. Groningen and her crew began 2016 with a period of rest after returning from the anti-piracy mission Atalanta. Zr.Ms. Groningen was deployed there as the first Ocean Going Patrol Vessel to combat piracy in the Gulf of Aden. Also in 2016, Zr.Ms. Groningen awaited a first. The ship was scheduled to participate in the EU operation FRONTEX in the Mediterranean in May and June. FRONTEX ensures proper border control and aims to prevent illegal trade in goods, weapons, and people. Before the ship would depart for the Mediterranean, it first sailed towards the fjords of Norway. Here, exercises were conducted in an international context with various submarines aimed at training submarine commanders. In addition to conducting simulated attacks on the submarines, Zr.Ms. Groningen was deployed to retrieve practice torpedoes from the water. During this three-week journey, two port visits were made to the Norwegian port city of Bergen. The spring was marked by a significant personnel change. A significant portion of the crew that had participated in Atalanta had since taken on other roles and had therefore been relieved. On March 11, kltz W.A. Hansen was also relieved after a command of 3.5 years. Kltz H.M. Sinke took over command and would prepare the ship for participation in FRONTEX. Zr.Ms. Groningen would be the first major surface unit of the Dutch Navy to participate in FRONTEX. The ship's task was to patrol south of Italy to monitor migrant flows and, where necessary, to bring migrants to safety when they were in distress. However, the mission changed due to a new prioritization, into a counter-drug operation of four months in the Caribbean from June to September. In a short period, the ship and crew were prepared for their West deployment. Groningen departed on June 5 from Den Helder to sail towards the Caribbean via the Azores. For its mission, the ship was equipped with an NH-90 onboard helicopter with an accompanying flight crew. Additionally, a team of marines came on board, as well as team members from the Caribbean Coast Guard and the U.S. Coast Guard. Even before the ship entered its first Caribbean port, it intercepted four hundred kilograms of drugs. A day earlier, the naval ship inspected a distressed sailing boat, whose crew had already been brought to safety shortly before. It turned out to be a successful deployment, during which nearly three thousand kilograms of drugs were intercepted and two search and rescue operations were conducted. Upon returning to Den Helder, one of the two main propulsion engines of the ship exhibited a technical failure. This led to additional maintenance being required in the autumn.

Dijkhuizen 2016 was primarily marked for Zr.Ms. Holland by the completion of the Named Maintenance and the successful execution of a training trajectory, followed by deployment in the Caribbean. In February, the ship completed the first phase of the training trajectory and could safely operate on board. The following period saw the ship gradually prepared for departure to sea. In March, the second phase of the training trajectory was completed, after which Zr.Ms. Holland set sail in April for the third phase: safe navigation. During this time, it also made a port visit to Antwerp. By early June, it completed the fourth phase, during which both safe navigation and operational deployment were tested, and a port visit to Oslo was made. At the end of June, Zr.Ms. Holland visited Amsterdam, where crew members welcomed their families on board for a sailing family day. During the training trajectory, a major defect occurred in the main propulsion diesel on the port side. During the months of July and August, this issue was repaired to ensure the ship was ready for deployment in the West. At the end of August, sea trials took place, and the ship was technically ready for departure. However, due to the repairs, Zr.Ms. Holland was unable to complete the final phase of its training trajectory as planned in July. This final phase still needed to be executed before the ship could cross the Atlantic Ocean. The patrol ship departed on September 4 for its deployment in the Caribbean. Due to the still-to-be-completed training trajectory, a pre-deployment training in British waters was successfully conducted. The ship received the stamp of 'deployment-ready' and thus crossed the Atlantic Ocean. During the crossing, it quickly became apparent that it would be a remarkable journey. Several tropical storms arose and had to be avoided. One storm developed into a fierce hurricane named Matthew. Zr.Ms. Holland reached the Caribbean almost at the same time that this hurricane struck Haiti. The crew rapidly prepared to provide hurricane relief to the heavily affected island. Together with Zr.Ms. Pelikaan, the ship transported 450 tons of aid supplies to the coastal areas of Haiti. During this deployment, the naval ship primarily focused on alleviating human suffering and laying a solid foundation for other aid organizations to build upon. After the deployment in Haiti, the patrol ship conducted over a month of coast guard operations in cooperation with the Coast Guard Caribbean Area. During this period, the naval ship intercepted a Venezuelan drug transport. Additionally, it played an important role in the ceremonial celebration of the 240th anniversary of the first international recognition of American independence by the Netherlands on Sint Eustatius. A fishing vessel in distress was also rescued and brought to safety, and Zr.Ms. Holland docked in Aruba. Marines stationed there embarked aid supplies, such as water and tents for Haiti.

FRISC Squadron Operational Deployment After a short preparation, in January 2016, a unit of five personnel was added to the Border Security Team (BST). This is an interdepartmental team that assists the Greek Coast Guard in processing the flow of migrants from Turkey. This support was part of FRONTEX, the European agency for the management of operational cooperation at the external borders. The BST was a new Dutch concept, consisting of personnel from the Royal Marechaussee, port police, customs, and the Royal Netherlands Navy. In this successful concept, a FRISC was chosen to patrol the territorial border between Turkey and Greece. This enabled early detection of migrants. Ultimately, hundreds of boat migrants were rescued, and arrests were made of individuals suspected of human smuggling. Manaslu Expedition In 2016, a unit from the Marine Corps climbed one of the world's highest mountains, Manaslu (8,163 m) in Nepal. As climbing high mountains falls within the expertise of the JKCMOX, Mountain Leaders from the JKCMOX supported the expedition. In preparation, several mandatory risk-mitigating activities were established for all participants, such as mandatory participation in the Alpine project in 2015, a medical examination, avalanche cases, a week of team building, and a simulated altitude activity in the pressure chamber of the Center for Humans and Aviation (CML). The expedition was also meteorologically prepared in close collaboration with the Joint Meteorology Group. By reaching the summit on May 9, 2016, the Mountain Leaders of the Marine Corps made Dutch history 60 years after the first ascent: the first military expedition to a mountain higher than 8,000 meters.

Particularly due to the unplanned deployment of Zr.Ms. Luymes for the Adelborsten Cruise and due to failures from various defects, it was not possible to achieve the required hydrographic days for this year. A total of 187 hydrographic days were realized. Maritime Environmental Information Centre In the past year, the METOC and Hydro seariders participated in various training sessions, exercises, and operations: the HQ weeks aboard Zr.Ms. Rotterdam, Cold Response, Joint Warrior, Emerald Move, BALTOPS, Sophia, SNMG1, and Atalanta (added to the international CTF465 staff). During the Cold Response exercise, they mainly provided environmental data and customized products. Hydrographic deployment is not always possible as part of an exercise scenario, but during Emerald Move, several beaches south of Sardinia were mapped for amphibious landings. Outside of all exercises and operations, a recording campaign was conducted in the Caribbean in the fall of 2016 with personnel from the MEIC and the HOVs. The plan is to continue this in the coming years. The recording campaign was interrupted to support the Human Disaster Relief Operation Haiti after Hurricane Matthew. The hydrographic team and recording system were embarked on Zr.Ms. Holland to conduct hydrographic REA operations along the Haitian coast. The ports of Port-au-Prince, Miragoane, Jeremy, and Les Cayes were mapped with the new MHP2 survey package. The MEIC not only provided searider support. Many operations and exercises were supported with specific products, such as Environmental Briefing Dockets (EBD) and Additional Military Layers (AML). Additionally, several missions were supported with very specific information deliveries, including for the Harpoon Trials, the MCM Work-Up, the LFAPS trials, and Torpedo Firing eXercises (TFX) southwest of Great Britain. These missions required custom-made products that integrated as much information as possible to provide a complete picture of the prevailing conditions. Support and Capacity Building The Hydrographic Service was also able to provide support for hydrographic education in 2016, for example, by allowing students from the Ocean Technology (Hydrography) program at the Maritime Institute Willem Barentsz to sail with HOVs. The REMUS course held in Ostend for the Defense Diving Group and the Mine Service also received support from a hydrographer this year. Equipment Just like in 2015, the management of hydrographic quality standards remained a continuous source of concern in 2016. Throughout 2016, the service continuously assisted the DMO and DMI organization in efforts to maintain the material condition of hydrographic and METOC equipment within CZSK according to the prevailing qualitative standards. In 2016, a new hydrographic network was established aboard the HOVs, including a data server with greater capacity, faster network connections, and new recording and processing PCs. With this modernization, fast data transfer and good data storage are guaranteed for the near future. For the first time in 2016, Ellipsoid Referenced Surveying (ERS) was used on the HOVs. With ERS, it is possible to reference the measured GPS antenna height to a Zr.Ms. Snellius.

Operations Directorate The Operations Directorate has accurately established an ellipsoidal reference surface. With the availability of the Ellipsoid-LAT difference surface, a result of research from Delft University of Technology, a direct link between GPS height and the LAT reduction surface is now possible. In this way, measured depths can be directly referenced to LAT, without the need for tide measurements. To enable the ERS technique, the latest GNSS techniques have also been utilized. With the use of new GNSS receivers and a correction signal, the Hydrographic Surveyors (HOV) now have a very precise positioning capability at the decimeter level. In 2016, the need to replace the current Side Scan Sonars with a new system was approved. This means that in 2017, the replacement of the current systems can begin. This replacement ensures object detection during hydrographic surveys for the near future and allows the ships to continue meeting the requirements of the International Hydrographic Organization.

Military Personnel Despite a tight personnel situation, the hydrographic and METOC personnel have been deployed multiple times for missions, training, and large exercises, see deployment MEIC (2.4). Their specialization and expertise are highly valuable and contribute significantly to the success of missions and exercises. Retaining this knowledge and expertise requires continuous attention, given the tight personnel situation combined with the limited training budget.

Civil Production In addition to regular production work, significant efforts were made in 2016 to complete the SHIP2 project. The topics Bathymetry and Spatial Data Infrastructures have been finalized. Additionally, the Civil Production section was closely involved in the preparations for ISO certification. Personnel were trained as internal auditors or contributed to the creation of process descriptions. Work was also done on a quality workbook, which describes work instructions. A total of 53 new ENC cells were published, along with 9 paper nautical charts for the corresponding area. Furthermore, a new edition of HP1 The Netherlands Coast Pilot was released, along with the annual editions of HP7, HP1D, HP33, and HP33D. In total, 462 "Notices to Mariners" were published. After reaching an agreement with Belgian colleagues on a more logical map layout of the joint surveying area around the Western Scheldt, these new products were prepared in 2016. Publication of these will follow in January 2017. In the context of IHO, participation occurred in the Hydrographic Standards and Services Committee (HSSC) and various related working groups: Nautical Cartography Working Group, Nautical Information Provision WG, Electronic Navigational Charts WG, and the S100 WG. A major focus is the development of standards for data exchange based on S100 (the Universal Hydrographic Data Model). Furthermore, the section was represented at the IC-ENC Technical Working Group in Taunton and held working meetings with colleagues from neighboring countries. One colleague also attended the CARIS world tour in Bologna, Italy. At the request of the Ministry of Infrastructure and Water Management, a staff member from the Service (the head of Data Management) participated in a working group under the Sub-Committee on Navigation, Communications and Search and Rescue (NCSR) of the International Maritime Organization (IMO). This working group assessed proposals for routing measures submitted by IMO member states. The service participates as a subject matter expert.

Geodesy and Tides The Knowledge Center for Geodesy & Tides (KCG&G) provides expertise for the measurement processes and publications of the Hydrographic Service, as well as for other branches of Defense and the government. The geodetic expertise is applied at sea, where water levels are of great importance. Tide knowledge is linked to marine geodesy. An important application is determining the correct coordinate systems and enabling conversions between them. This concerns both horizontal and vertical references. The choice of a system affects the calculation of points, lines, and areas. Another application is providing geodetic and tide data for general use, such as calculating boundaries at sea and publishing tide predictions.

142 143 Directorate Operations Directorate Operations areas therefore have earlier issues with unfavorable loading conditions, such as high seas. Poor weather conditions caused the ship to return. On February 7, the ship entered Den Helder again. On February 9, the A-crew departed to sea for loading operations, and then on February 13 sailed to Zeebrugge, Belgium. In Zeebrugge, it conducted a Continuation Training (CT) for a week to enhance the level and competence of the crew. The Belgian-Dutch MOST led and provided the training. During this period, maneuvering, navigation, and fire drills were conducted, among others. The training period lasted until Friday, February 19, and resulted in a Satisfactory rating. The ship was to continue its way to the operational area for the execution of loading operations; however, these could not proceed again due to poor weather conditions. Therefore, the ship docked again in Den Helder on Monday, February 22. The B-crew set sail that same Monday for two weeks of loading operations. During this period, an ash scattering at sea was conducted. A select group carried out the ceremony with attention and respect, and a minute of silence was observed. Photos of the ceremony were taken for the home front. After the period of loading operations, the B-crew returned to the port of Den Helder on March 7. On the same day, the A-crew departed for a week of loading operations. A week later, they briefly returned to Den Helder to pick up a new navtex, before resuming loading operations at sea. A navtex provides the ship with necessary navigational and meteorological information and is required to be present on the bridge. Due to the bad weather, not much loading was done, but they mainly waited in the area for better conditions. On Monday, March 21, the A-crew returned. With this, they also completed their last voyage on Zr.Ms. Luymes for 2016. That same Monday, the B-crew set sail to conduct loading and wreck contact research. During this, the found wrecks in the area were further and accurately examined to determine the least water depth. On March 26, a tide gauge buoy that had been laid the previous year was picked up. This buoy with a sensor on the bottom measures water levels. By measuring this for a period of months, an accurate tide measurement and prediction can be made. On Sunday, March 27, they docked again in Den Helder. Between Monday, April 4, and Wednesday, May 11, the B-crew conducted loading operations, during which a few days were planned to be in Den Helder. This period went quite efficiently as the weather was good and the ship performed well technically and hydrographically. During this period, a tide gauge buoy was also streamed, and wreck contact research was again on the agenda. On Tuesday, May 17, the ship departed to load until May 19. The short duration of this period was due to the fact that the ship unexpectedly had to participate in the Adelborsten Cruise. For this, the ship was prepared in a very short time for an intensive six-week voyage. This posed a considerable challenge that was taken on with much enthusiasm by the crew. On Monday, May 23, a large group of cadets embarked for the Adelborsten Cruise, and Zr.Ms. Luymes, with the B-crew, set course for Ostend. Throughout the entire cruise, a Weekly Practice Program (WPP) was maintained. Together with the Belgian ship BNS Godetia, they anchored on May 24 at Vlissingen. A day after anchoring, the ships advanced towards Ostend. Along the way, various exercises were conducted, including helicopter operations with the Allouette from BNS Godetia and towing and RAS approaches with Zr.Ms. Schiedam and the aforementioned Belgian ship. On Friday, May 27, they docked alongside BNS Godetia in Ostend, where a festive weekend, 'Oostende voor Anker', was taking place. The crew and the cadets were able to enjoy themselves here after an intensive first week of the cruise. Early on Sunday, May 29, the weekend came to an end, and they departed for Berga, Sweden. Along the way, the lock in Brunsbüttel had to be passed. The ship then sailed through the Nord-Ostsee Canal to the Holtenau lock near Kiel and then further into the Baltic Sea towards Berga. Along the way, various exercises were regularly conducted together with Zr.Ms. Schiedam and BNS Godetia, including a Force Protection exercise and an NBCD carousel on board the ships themselves. On Friday, June 3, they docked in Berga, a naval base in Sweden. This port was filled with ships participating in the large exercise BALTOPS. After a short port visit, they set sail again on Sunday, June 5, towards Stockholm. However, Zr.Ms. Luymes fell outside the BALTOPS program due to the sudden involvement in the cruise. Therefore, the ship organized its own program with various exercises.

This week also had many exercises planned, including a hoisting exercise with the Alouette from BNS Godetia, RAS approaches, and a maneuvering exercise with small vessels. During the open days that weekend, the line for other ships turned out to be just a bit longer than for Zr.Ms. Luymes; apparently, a hydrographic ship is less interesting than the Chinese or Spanish frigate that was positioned in front of and behind the Dutch ship. On Monday, June 20, the ship departed from Kiel with new cadets on board. It immediately set course for the Little Belt to conduct navigation exercises. This area was perfect for this purpose due to the many visual entry and exit marks. On the way, a hoisting exercise was conducted with an NH90 from the Danish Coast Guard. At night, the Great Belt was crossed to then continue the route around the north through the Oresund towards Copenhagen. On Wednesday, a large shooting exercise was held with moving targets at a Danish shooting range. On Thursday, despite the rain, the barbecue could still take place. The following morning, Friday, June 24, it docked in Aalborg. After yet another last port of the cruise, the ship departed on Monday, June 27, for the final week with Den Helder as the end destination. On the way, Tromøysundet was visited for the photex. This beautiful area is located in a kind of fjord. After a rough journey across the North Sea characterized by bad weather and high waves, Den Helder was entered on Thursday, June 30. The sailing family day planned for the next day unfortunately had to be canceled due to the circumstances. This marked an early end to the Cadet Cruise. On July 15, the C crew departed for the first time with Zr.Ms. Luymes to sea for loading operations and wreck contact investigation. Luymes was in Aberdeen from Thursday, August 11, to Sunday, August 14, for a routine port visit. After this port visit, the rest of the week was spent loading until the day of entry. On Monday, August 22, the C crew went to sea for loading operations until September 5. On September 5, the B crew departed for loading operations. This time, there were special guests on board, namely students from the Willem Barentsz college. These students from the Maritime School Terschelling study Hydrography, and for them, this was an excellent opportunity to experience real work on a Hydrographic platform. Halfway through the sailing period, the first group disembarked, and new students came on board. This boat transfer was conducted above Terschelling. On September 19, the ship docked in Den Helder. This was the last trip for the B crew on Zr.Ms. Luymes. The C crew manned the ship until the end of the year. On Monday, September 19, the C crew undocked the ship. During this period, loading operations were carried out, with a routine port visit to the British city of Middlesbrough in between, before entering Den Helder on Wednesday, September 28. On Monday, October 3, the C crew departed for the last loading days of the year. On Thursday, October 6, the ship arrived in Den Helder for major scheduled maintenance. Directorate of Material Maintenance Directorate of Material Maintenance Following the transfer of the historical 'De Voorwerf' in 2015, on January 11, 2016, the strip along the Oosterdok with buildings 022, 023, 024, and 027 (E-wing) was transferred to the Rijksvastgoed Bedrijf. The Project Bureau Marine Terrein Amsterdam took over its management and will carry out the redevelopment of the area on behalf of the state and the municipality. On the same day, the Minister of Housing and the National Service Stef Blok and the Mayor of Amsterdam Eberhard van der Laan opened a bicycle and pedestrian bridge over the Dijksgracht. This command bridge provides a direct connection between Kattenburgerplein and the Dijksgracht. The staff had already moved into the Provoosthuis (building 015) in November 2015. Originally, this was to be for a maximum duration of 1 year, but the planned relocation to building 012 has been postponed and may take place at the end of 2017. In addition to the EU presidency and the evacuation and relocation issues, the reorganization of various defense components and the implementation of SAP for shore establishments also played an important role this year. The consequences of this were clearly noticeable, as the facility and logistical processes within Defense are still undergoing changes. Nevertheless, the establishment, together with local supporters such as DBBO, PARESTO, and FBD, once again demonstrated in 2016 what the Marine Etablissement Amsterdam can and means for CZSK, Defense, the city of Amsterdam, society, and of course this year also for the European Union. Two of the crew members of the MEA, MATR 1 OD S. Jansen and MATR 1 OD A. Meerman, risked their lives this winter to rescue a drowning person from the IJ. For this, they were awarded the Blue Honor Ribbon and a reward, respectively. Events in 2016 In the first half of 2016, only smaller events could take place due to support for the EU presidency. Although the event center was closed in the first half of the year, visitor numbers decreased, but less than expected. This was mainly due to more intensive use of other facilities. However, from the summer period, operations could resume at full capacity. The last four months of the year saw visitor numbers nearly the same as in previous years. The total number of visitors this year was 17,639, during 776 events. The Marine Etablissement Amsterdam is still one of the few defense locations with flexible large hall capacity. Its central location in the Netherlands, the city center of Amsterdam within walking distance, and proximity to international entry and exit points make the barracks an extremely suitable and unique location for discussion forums, symposia, and presentations within the international defense community. In addition to the Golf World Cup, we were responsible for various large NATO conferences and symposia, including the CHANCOM: the meeting of all NATO naval commanders from the area around the Channel and the North Sea. Furthermore, the Marine Etablissement Amsterdam was once again the host location for BeNeSaM discussions between the Belgian Command Council and the Dutch Admiralty Council. New this year was the shared use of the conference facilities by civil partners, introduced by the Project Bureau Marine Terrein Amsterdam. Accommodation This year, 15,845 reservations for Short-Term Accommodation were processed for activities on and around the Marine Etablissement Amsterdam. Port Visits The number of port visits remained nearly the same this year. The largest applicants continue to be the port and towing service Den Helder and DDG. In many cases, a port visit was made to Amsterdam as part of a transit, but also to a greater extent for deployment in support of national authorities. This year, several foreign visits also occurred. Entrance Europagebouw. The building is beautifully illuminated in colors.

Van Braam Houckgeest Barracks Commander: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) drs. J.P.S.M. de Rooij After a longer period without a First Officer, the new officer took office at the beginning of January. Crucial in this was the change of the Head of Logistics, a position that was not filled again for several months. The organization recognized that the barracks accommodation in particular had been in need of improvement over the years. However, for the storage issue, it was necessary to resort to Maartensdijk. In terms of maintenance, the outdated condition of the barracks continued to take its toll. During an IL&T inspection in August, covering both the Van Braam Houckgeest Barracks and Maartensdijk, several minor deficiencies were identified. Fortunately, these could be quickly remedied. Nevertheless, due to the results of the inspection in Den Helder, all of CZSK was placed under intensified supervision. Main building of the Van Braam Houckgeest Barracks, Doorn.

Directorate of Material Maintenance Directorate of Material Maintenance was officially transferred from DMO to CZSK with the unveiling of the nameplates Noordzee, Waddenzee, and Zuiderzee. Three captains (ktz) were fully trained and authorized to deploy the Noordzee-class for towing operations by mid-2016. The plan is for the two remaining captains to be fully trained by early 2017, resulting in five operational crews for the Noordzee-class from that point onward. In the months following the transfer, four tugboats of the Lingeklasse: Regge, Linge, Hunze, and Rotte, were decommissioned. The Gouwe is then the only remaining Lingeklasse tugboat that is part of the fleet. In addition to the fact that the operation of the Noordzee-class is very different compared to the Lingeklasse, the maintenance system was also significantly changed. This maintenance was structurally carried out at a civilian shipyard. The warranty period of the three boats has shown that civilian outsourcing of maintenance has so far yielded positive experiences. The second major theme within the product group was the optimization of operations. The goal was to facilitate the operational fleet as effectively as possible with the available resources. There was a continuous tension between the available personnel from the towing service and harbor watchmen (Steiger 19), various tasks, and a continuously fluctuating workload that is visible in the short term. The many ship-related activities such as dock planning, oil loading and unloading planning, ammunition loading and unloading planning, tours, practical lesson planning, responding to extreme weather conditions, and the deployment of tugboat crews posed a constant challenge for the Harbor Operations and Coordination Center (HOCC) and resulted in a dynamic planning process. The aim is to continue improving this process. In addition to coordinating and planning, active support was provided multiple times to the National Police, and civil-military cooperation with Port of Den Helder was continued. The Traffic Center (VTS) Den Helder registered more than 50,000 ship movements in 2016. The traffic management, which makes traffic decisions on behalf of the Rijkswaterstaat to ensure safe and smooth shipping movements, underwent several personnel changes, including the promotion of one of the former traffic managers to the position of Deputy Head of Traffic Service. Additionally, two candidates completed the training to become traffic managers; one of them is already a traffic manager, while the other will be ready early next year. The harbor watchmen (Steiger 19) played an essential role in the (un)mooring of ships. The small team, consisting of three employees in 2016, experienced a personnel change with the departure of a permanent staff member. Despite the highly fluctuating workload, the harbor watchmen made it possible for many vessels to enter the Waddenzee, the second tugboat of the new Noordzee-class, from Romania. Bridge of the Waddenzee.

Veldhuizen In 2016, the main task of accommodating CZSK ship crews was not fulfilled. However, tasks shifted this year towards a more general-facilitating defense location. As a result, the two core tasks for Naval Base Vlissingen consisted of logistical support for a large number of exercises for CZSK units and other military components, and collaborating and networking with government agencies and the business sector for the new barracks to be built in 2021. The closing date of Naval Base Vlissingen has been moved from July 1, 2017, to April 1, 2018. This year, various units were accommodated at the base for battlefield tours. Among others, the MAROST (Maritime Support) staff, the Middle Defense Education (MDV), various CLAS units, and the Royal Marines (UK) were guests. The VeVa training program set up its camp at MKVLIS for a week in mid-2016, and the Certifex of the Marine Corps took place here in June. For a DBBO training this fall, accommodation was offered at MKVLIS due to a shortage of lodging at airbase Woensdrecht. Besides providing accommodation and food, the base was frequently visited throughout the year for theme days from the Zeeland Safety Region and consortia Michiel Adriaanszoon de Ruyterkazerne (MARKAZ), DSI, meetings, reunions (former crew members, COM, AVOM, BNMO, BOSS), and receptions. It also provided logistical support for festivities for the anniversary year, such as the tenth edition of ‘Rescue Vlissingen’ held in the summer. Permanent office and other facilities were provided to the staff of Defense Suppliers Oversight from DMO, 30 National Reserve (NATRES) battalion A-company, and a support team from CLSK. Week 19 was characterized by peak activity, as various components and agencies made use of the facilities. Additionally, the Customs Harmony practiced for two days at the base for a tattoo, and the 17th Armored Infantry Battalion, with 120 personnel, stayed there in preparation for the CLAS days in Goes. On Thursday, May 12, an information meeting was organized by RVB/PO-MARKAZ for potential entrepreneurs in the forming consortia. The Commander and the Head of Logistics attended the New Year's receptions of various municipalities in Walcheren. They also attended various commemorations and wreath-laying ceremonies, including the Remembrance of the Dead on May 4, commemorations in Kapelle, Vlissingen (Uncle Beach/Battle of the Scheldt), and Bergen op Zoom (Canadays). Furthermore, they attended the Zeeland Veterans Day, networking days of the Safety Region, the Prinsjesfestival, former contact days, and meetings of various institutions. The highlight was the awarding of the ‘Franklin D. Roosevelt Four Freedoms Award’ to German Chancellor Angela Merkel on April 21 in Middelburg. The closing date of the barracks was postponed in 2016. This is related to a delay in the realization of the new barracks, which is now scheduled for completion in 2021. On June 22, an important agreement was signed on board Zr.Ms. De Ruyter during a port visit to the city of Vlissingen. This agreement between the Ministry of Defense, the province of Zeeland, the municipality of Vlissingen, and the Water Board specifically concerned agreements regarding the territory. During the nighttime exercise LOWLANDS 2016, a Medevac Cougar picked up "wounded" in Vlissingen.

Product group energy distribution company Head: Ms. Drs. A.M. Valent-Groot The Energy Distribution Company has been the energy supplier and network manager for defense locations in Den Helder since 1957. With its own power plant, the Combined Heat and Power Station, electricity is generated, and the heat released is used to provide approximately half of the buildings at the Nieuwe Haven with warmth. Across the defense sector, the Energy Distribution Company manages contracts and invoice control for electricity, gas, and water. It also addresses demand requests and reports consumption figures, which are used to provide advice on reducing energy use. In 2016, it was 100 years since shore power was first supplied to a ship of the Royal Netherlands Navy in Den Helder. This means the Navy is far ahead of civil shipping, which has only recently begun to adopt shore power. With funds from the Van der Staaij Motion, a new employee for Integrated Safety and Quality was appointed at the EDB in April. This allowed for better compliance with safety, security, and environmental requirements within the EDB. In the same month, the assortment management of Energy and Water was formally transferred from the CDC to the EDB. The work had been carried out by the EDB since 2005. May 12 was a special day for the EDB. For the first time in 100 years of shore power, a ship returned power to the shore. Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman had, in parallel with the KWS, supplied electricity to the EDB electricity grid. If necessary, the Karel Doorman can supply electricity to ships or to the shore, for example during maintenance of the generators on board or in exceptional circumstances, such as in aid to areas affected by a natural disaster. In June, the site lighting along the Koegraszeedijk was replaced with LED lighting. After the closing time of the Zuidpoort, the lighting is dimmed. Particularly, dimming contributes to energy savings compared to traditional site lighting. Lieutenant Colonel (ltkolmarns) P.J. Baijards and project leader P.W. Terpstra took the first charging stations for electric cars into use.

General At 8,000 kilometers from the Netherlands, the navy is in full motion. Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Training and Support A variety of exercises and training sessions took place in the Caribbean over the past year. This was to maintain the operational readiness of the own units, but also served as an ideal training location for CZSK, CLSK, and CLAS units or partners in the region. Naval Training Vessel Van Kinsbergen The naval training vessel (MOV) Van Kinsbergen is used for nautical practical training. The ship was specifically built and equipped for this purpose. It accommodates sixteen trainees. In addition to the regular navigation bridge, the Van Kinsbergen has a fully equipped secondary training bridge. The ship is suitable for safely practicing mooring and unmooring maneuvers and is equipped with a RHIB. Each year, the Van Kinsbergen sails for approximately 200 days. The main user is the KIM. The ship is deployed to teach future naval officers practical nautical skills necessary to work as a watch officer on the bridge of a naval vessel. Additionally, the ship also has a formative function, focusing on team building and character development. The ship is used as a supplement to theory and (bridge) simulator lessons. It is also deployed during the annual sailing period, during which a longer training voyage of about five weeks is undertaken together with a flotilla of minehunters; the cruise. Besides the KIM, the Operational School is also a major user. For this, practical sailing sessions are provided for the training of non-commissioned officers' sailing qualifications for minehunters. Marines also learn to operate landing craft with it. Future navigation officers receive various training on board, such as mooring and unmooring. Civil maritime schools also make good use of the Van Kinsbergen for training future maritime officers. Technical training on board is also possible. Upon request, bridge teams from individual ships can use the Van Kinsbergen for tailored training or as part of a training trajectory. Occasionally, the ship is used for scientific research (TNO, universities) or for informational purposes. MOV Van Kinsbergen Jan-Dec For a few years now, the Van Kinsbergen has been sailing with a fixed schedule aligned with the Vocational Technical Education (VTO) periods. As a result, January of each year begins with the first sailing weeks for the beginning midshipmen on the Van Kinsbergen. The VTO period lasts a total of two years, during which these midshipmen undertake a sea service practicum (ZPR) on board the Van Kinsbergen three times for one week. The last ZPR lasts two weeks. The sailing week, together with a week on the Ship Handling Simulator (SHS), concludes a theoretical block. This allows for a progressive learning line to be realized, where the knowledge gained from the previous block serves as the basis for the subsequent block. This is also reflected in the program designed for the midshipmen. ZPR 1 is filled with the elementary aspects of navigation, such as learning to determine a position; evasive maneuvers; taking bearings; the operation of a 'leading line', and to break the week, a port visit. This is necessary to allow the midshipmen to process all the knowledge gained, but also to take a break; especially the night watch and the 24-hour operational concept can be quite challenging for most midshipmen. This is also the moment to provide the midshipman with summative feedback on their performance thus far. In 2015/2016, there was a transitional year. To better align the programs of both the KIM and the KMA, it was decided to conduct the VTO education for both the Long Officer Training (LOO) and the Short Officer Training (KOO) over one and a half years. This resulted in the LOO that started in 2014 still falling under the old arrangement and only beginning the VTO in the second year, while the new intake of 2015 also started the VTO education. Consequently, there was a 50 percent increase in students, workload, and sailing days for the first half of 2016. The four sailing weeks per block were therefore extended to six sailing weeks per block.

Just before the summer leave, the Pelikaan once again provided transport for the CIDW to and from Bonaire. This transport was combined with support for a sniper training course from the Marine Training Center. Over several days, operational snipers from the Korps Mariniers and snipers in training were able to hone their skills in maritime sniping. After the summer leave, minor maintenance was carried out to ensure that all ship systems were functioning optimally again. This was immediately put to the test by supporting the visit of a unit from the United States Marine Corps Force Reconnaissance. In cooperation with the FRISC troop and other elements of the 32RSQN, the Pelikaan conducted amphibious training and practiced boat drills. The ship also served as a diving platform while logistical support was provided. 

On September 21, the transport of the CIDW from Bonaire was combined with a port visit and an open day. On this day, not only the Pelikaan visited the island, but also a cutter from the coast guard, the CURMIL, the KMar, and the CIDW were present during the open day. A large number of island residents, particularly several classes of elementary school students, visited the units and enjoyed the demonstrations. In the following week, a tropical disturbance developed over the Atlantic Ocean. This intensified to hurricane strength heading towards the Caribbean. Upon reaching the easternmost Caribbean islands, the forecast indicated that this hurricane Matthew would find its way to the Lesser Antilles. All units of the Commander of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean prepared for a passage of the Lesser Antilles. Ultimately, Matthew passed as a Category 3 hurricane about two hundred miles north of the Lesser Antilles. The expected damage in Curaçao did not occur. Aruba and Bonaire particularly experienced extreme rainfall. 

On Monday, October 10, the Pelikaan departed with aid supplies, vehicles, and additional personnel towards heavily affected Haiti. The first stop was Aruba to pick up the marines from 32RSQN, along with extra supplies and vehicles. From October 10 to 30, the ship was deployed in close cooperation with marines from the 32RSQN to provide aid supplies to the most severely affected villages along the coast. The Pelikaan visited Port-au-Prince multiple times to take on aid supplies from various aid organizations. The crew members and marines then distributed the goods with the FRISC’s and carried out recovery projects in the affected villages. Government representatives and representatives from aid organizations were also on board to ensure that aid supplies reached the right places and could be distributed safely and in a coordinated manner. By the end of October, most communities had received emergency aid, and aid organizations took over the further structural rebuilding. The Pelikaan returned via Aruba to Curaçao for a week of leave. Due to the deployment in Haiti after the passage of Matthew, the planned transport weeks could not take place. However, there was a need for several goods in the Windward Islands. From November 14 to 22, the Pelikaan provided transport for these goods, including Super RHIBS for the coast guard. This week was combined with a port visit to San Juan, Puerto Rico, which partially coincided with the visit of the then-station ship Zr.Ms. Holland. Immediately after returning, Minister of Defense Jeanine Hennis-Plasschaert visited Curaçao. On Wednesday, November 23, she presented several medals to crew members of Zr.Ms. Pelikaan for their efforts after the hurricane passage on the island of Dominica, one year earlier. After a week in port, the Pelikaan provided support from December 5 to 15 during the emergency aid operation in Haiti, moored next to Zr.Ms. Holland. Shelter boxes were ready on the helideck of the Holland.
