Emergency Situations

In emergency situations on ships, the Coast Guard is called for assistance. Examples of these situations include when a ship has run aground, has had a collision, or has become unmanageable. The Coast Guard is reachable 24 hours a day via various communication lines. In 2016, 2,340 emergency and urgent reports were received, of which 538 were unintentional.

Inland Vessel Sunk

The Coast Guard Center (KWC) received a report on July 5, 2016, of a sinking inland vessel on the IJsselmeer. The KWC summoned the Coast Guard aircraft, a rescue helicopter, and six rescue boats to provide assistance. There were three people on board, who were in the wheelhouse. This had filled with water, causing one crew member to become hypothermic. The crew members were brought ashore at Stavoren and treated by ambulance personnel once there.

Coast Guard Enforcement

To ensure safe and smooth processing of maritime traffic in the North Sea, the Coast Guard supervises compliance with applicable traffic and behavioral regulations. Enforcement officers at the Coast Guard Coordination and Communication Center carry out this task. They take action based on information from computer systems or direct Coast Guard units to conduct inspections or controls and take enforcement action. Although much information is available through various automated systems, surveillance using ships, aircraft, and helicopters provides important additional (detailed) information about, for example, potentially criminal discharges of polluted wastewater or oil. In 2016, a total of 34 criminal discharges were observed according to the criteria of the Bonn Agreement Report. Customs officers and members of the Royal Marechaussee work together on board the Coast Guard patrol vessels to inspect ships in the North Sea. Together with the Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA), the Coast Guard checks fishing logs, catch composition, storage space, and prohibited net equipment. In 2016, 1,218 inspections were carried out, resulting in 254 criminal offenses being detected and 172 reports being drawn up. There were 36 warnings issued and 16 administrative measures taken.

SAR Operation Becomes Drug Case

A fishing boat encountered problems on the evening of January 14, 2016, during a severe storm and sent out a distress signal. Various units were immediately alerted. It was not until the course of the night that the crew could be rescued at the mouth of the Westerschelde after a joint effort by the Coast Guard, the Belgian Air Force, and the Royal Netherlands Rescue Society (KNRM). Due to the bad weather, the boat could not be towed, and the wreck washed ashore at Cadzand during the night. When Customs officers, together with the police, boarded the wreck, they made a remarkable discovery: one thousand kilograms of cocaine.

Reorganization of the Technical Domain RN (HTD)  
Project Leader: Captain (ktz) ir. J.W. Hartman  

The Royal Netherlands Navy has the ambition to remain an innovative navy in the future, even with scarce technical personnel, increasing technical complexity, and limited financial resources, while ensuring its material readiness effectively. To achieve this goal, the program for the Reorganization of the Technical Domain RN (HTD) was initiated in 2013 after thorough research. An important first step in the HTD program was the merger of the Technical Service (TD) and the Armament Technical Service (WD). This step took place on May 7, 2014. With the merger, the existing personnel was consolidated into one service, the Technical Service (TD). In 2016, various projects and trials aimed at changing the technical operations on board the operational units and streamlining training were completed, and the results were subsequently integrated into the line organization. Furthermore, the reorganization plan was established to optimally align the job profile for TD personnel with the changes brought about by the HTD program. This was done after extensive consultation with employee representation and trade unions. The implementation of the reorganization will start in 2017. With the integration of the results into the line organization and the upcoming implementation of the reorganization in 2017, the HTD program in its current form has been terminated, and the further development of the TD will be shaped within the TD committee, the advisory body of the Flag Officer Technical Service.

Coast Guard Netherlands
Director: Captain (ktz) R.J. Blok MSc

The Coast Guard protects and promotes the responsible use of the North Sea and monitors the Dutch borders, but it does not do this alone. The Coast Guard operates on behalf of five ministries: Infrastructure and Water Management, Defence, Security and Justice, Finance, and Economic Affairs. In 2016, Coast Guard personnel, together with staff from the participating services – Rijkswaterstaat, Royal Netherlands Navy, Police, Customs, Royal Marechaussee, Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority, Royal Air Force, Inspectorate for the Environment and Transport, and the State Supervision of Mines – worked for the safety (safety & security) and economic interests of our country.

Steps towards modernization
For the Coast Guard, 2016 was a busy and challenging year. A year in which important decisions were made regarding the modernization of the Coast Guard, the reorganization came into effect, and the regular Coast Guard tasks in the areas of service provision and enforcement were carried out. The decision-making for the development and acquisition of the Maritime Operations Center Coast Guard, to replace the existing Coast Guard center, was an important step towards a modern and future-oriented Coast Guard that can operate information-driven and is equipped for its tasks.

Contribution to European operation 'Triton'
FRONTEX, the European agency for the management and coordination of external borders, requested the Netherlands to deploy the Coast Guard aircraft for the European operation Triton. Therefore, in April, the Coast Guard aircraft was stationed on the Italian island of Lampedusa to conduct surveillance over the Mediterranean Sea. The task of the aircraft and its crew was to detect and map illegal migration flows from North Africa to Europe during patrol flights, so that the responsible authorities could anticipate the situation. In case of emergencies, the aircraft could be requested to contribute to search and rescue activities, in accordance with international obligations.

Search and Rescue
Drowning victims, shipwrecked individuals, or others in distress or danger are located and rescued by the Coast Guard. Coast Guard ships, helicopters, and aircraft are ready for this Search and Rescue (SAR) task 24 hours a day. The Coast Guard carries out its SAR tasks in the North Sea (in the territorial sea and within the Dutch Exclusive Economic Zone), the Wadden Sea, the IJsselmeer, the Randmeren, and the South Holland and Zeeland rivers. In 2016, 1,565 assistance and rescue operations were carried out.

Missing kitesurfer
On October 5, 2016, the Coast Guard center in Den Helder coordinated a large-scale search operation for a missing kitesurfer. Based on various data, such as current and wind, the operators determined the search plan for the rescue units. Searching continued late into the night in the hope of finding the man alive. Unfortunately, the units found the lifeless body of the kitesurfer in Krabbendijke (Zeeland).

1_Navy_Annual_Report_2017_INTRO-TABLE OF CONTENTS-3 3 ANNUAL REPORT OF THE ROYAL NETHERLANDS NAVY 2017

In 2016, the navy was deployed in major international operations and exercises. Prominent this year was the provision of emergency aid. After the devastating force of Hurricane Matthew, Haiti was particularly in ruins, leading to significant shortages of basic necessities. Various ships set course for the affected country to provide assistance and deliver supplies. Marines also took action to ensure that the aid could be distributed safely among the population. Additionally, the navy showcased its capabilities in the Mediterranean by rescuing migrants in perilous situations at sea. As part of drug enforcement, several ships participated in the Counterdrug Operation Carib Venture. Furthermore, participation occurred in large international exercises such as Black Alligator and Emerald Move. The maintenance program for the Walrus-class submarines continued, and the maintenance of Zr.Ms. Van Speijk was successfully completed. Personnel underwent many new training courses and participated in (international) exercises. During the World Port Days in Rotterdam, the navy was present with marines and several ships to introduce visitors to the armed forces. Cover photo: Haiti, Les Cayes, October 11, 2016. The Dutch armed forces provide emergency aid to Haiti after Hurricane Matthew has ravaged the island. Participating ships of the Royal Netherlands Navy are Zr.Ms. Holland and Zr.Ms. Pelikaan. FOREWORD In your hands, you have the annual report of the Royal Netherlands Navy 2017. In this report, you can read about the deployments the navy undertook during extensive international operations and exercises, as well as the actions taken by the shore organization to facilitate these deployments. The Navy made a significant impression during SAIL and the Marine Days in Den Helder. Old sailing ships and new war vessels were simultaneously on display in and around the Nieuwe Haven. Additionally, marines landed with heavy equipment onshore for the interested public. With thousands of visitors, it was a great success and a wonderful opportunity to showcase what the Navy has to offer. Prominently featured in 2017 was emergency aid. After the devastating hurricane Irma, Sint Maarten was particularly in ruins and there were significant shortages of basic necessities. Various ships set course for the affected island to provide assistance and deliver supplies. Marines were also deployed to ensure that the aid could be distributed safely among the population. The personnel underwent many new training courses and participated in (international) exercises. At the World Port Days in Rotterdam, the navy was present with marines and ships to introduce visitors to the naval forces. We hope that this Yearbook will prove to be a useful reference work. 4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-4 23 Directorate Personnel and Operations Legal Affairs (JUZA) Head: Captain (ktz) mr. G. Souer The JUZA department is part of the DP&O, one of the five line directorates of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK). The department advises and supports CZSK, the directors of CZSK, and commanders of units on all legal issues that arise. JUZA provides legal advice and acts as a point of contact for the directors and commanders within CZSK. Additionally, JUZA monitors the legal and administrative diligence of operations within CZSK. The main areas of law that the department deals with include (military) criminal and disciplinary law, operational law, and state and administrative law. These areas of law are organized into three different bureaus. Thus, every employee at JUZA can function as a first point of contact (counter function) for questions directed to the department. JUZA does not provide legal advice to individual military personnel, but does assist them if necessary. In criminal or disciplinary matters, JUZA is primarily involved on the side of CZSK and the Ministry of Defence as an organization. Should a military member be involved in a criminal case, they can receive assistance from the Ministry of Defence in this matter. Personnel and Organization (P&O) In 2017, several important steps were taken within the Ministry of Defence that also had an impact on the Personnel and Organization (P&O) domain. It was decided to make the organization more adaptive, a start was made with DOKM, and in November an agreement was reached on a collective labor agreement for 2017-2018. As part of the Adaptive Armed Forces, the Bureau Flexible Capacity was established within P&O. This bureau originated from the Bureau Reservists. The latter agency was engaged until June in the deployment and administrative support of the reservists of the Royal Netherlands Navy Reserve. In addition to continuing this task, the Bureau Flexible Capacity was established as the coordinator for external hiring and deployment of temporarily available military and civilian personnel. In 2017, CZSK began with DOKM. A project organization was set up for this purpose. DOKM for CZSK involves: the expansion of operational (combat) support. In the coming years, these expansions will be implemented, which will lead to an increase in mine countermeasure capacity, the establishment of a Fleet Marine Squadron, and the construction of a Combat Support Ship.

4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-5 24 Directorate of Personnel and Operations After a long negotiation process, an agreement was reached at the end of November between the Defense leadership and the trade unions regarding a new Collective Labor Agreement for Defense. The biggest change is the new termination of service regulation, which links the retirement age to the AOW (state pension) age. Military personnel will now be dismissed five years before the AOW age. Working longer is no longer only the norm for civilian personnel, but also for military personnel. In 2017, the shortage of personnel (technical and operational) was painfully felt, resulting in many temporary transfers and replacements to meet the required deployment. The frequent transfers led to unrest, and in some cases, it was a reason for departure. To break this downward trend, it was decided to allow only voluntary replacements and to work on extending the duration of assignments where possible. Career Guidance Career guidance is the alignment of personnel wishes with the possibilities that the organization offers regarding career paths. This alignment takes place in the form of a career conversation, which is held during each function or once every three years. This conversation encompasses the personal developments of the involved official in the near future, as well as in the medium and long term. Personal development of the employee is necessary to remain valuable to the organization. In addition to this internal mobility, the career counselor pays attention to external mobility for employees who will not progress in the long term but will leave Defense. The career guidance section included four military offices for the operational service groups, Marines, technical service, and logistics service, and one office for civilian personnel. At the beginning of 2017, this section had 37 military and 3 civilian positions. Since mid-year, the career guidance office for civilian personnel has been fully staffed, allowing for career conversations for civilian personnel on a larger scale. Furthermore, as of October 1, career guidance for civilian personnel has been implemented and established across Defense. Integration (INT) The Integration department (INT) is part of the Directorate of Personnel and Operations (DPBV), one of the three line directorates of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK). The INT department aims to manage the operational and supporting process chains of the CZSK integrally on behalf of C-ZSK, focused on delivering deployable units in accordance with the assignment of the Chief of Defence Staff (CDS). The INT department consists of three bureaus: Bureau Strategy and Advice (S&A), Bureau Policy, Planning & Budgeting (BPB), and Bureau Investments (INV). Bureau Strategy & Advice The Bureau S&A supports C-ZSK in its role as maritime military advisor to the CDS and the Minister of Defence. Bureau S&A operates in two teams: the Advice team and the International Military Cooperation team. The Advice team acts as the first point of contact (mailbox) for the Executive Staff (Defence Staff and Main Directorates) regarding policy documents, studies, parliamentary matters, and the so-called Hague consultations. Important tasks this year included activities related to DOKM and the Defence Memorandum. This team also supported the Head of the Policy Directorate in the development of the 'Work Program Maritime Strategy & Ports 2018-2021', an interdepartmental work program initiated together with the Maritime Cluster based on the Maritime Strategy 2015 - 2025. Additionally, this team provides analysis of inspection reports from the Inspector General of the Armed Forces regarding visits to CZSK units. The International Military Cooperation (IMS) team supports C-ZSK in maintaining its international contacts and working relationships.

Bureau BPB is composed of three sections: Planning Integration (PLINT), Programs (PROG), and Material Support (MOST). The PLINT section is responsible for the integral planning process within CZSK. This year's training took place in Belize, which presents a significant challenge regarding communications due to the dense vegetation and the unpredictable nature of the terrain. NIMCIS Very High Frequency (VHF) and Ultra High Frequency (UHF) are virtually unusable here, making reliance solely on HF communications necessary. In response to the concerning situation regarding these communications during the last training in Belize in 2015, the JKCMOX requested extensive communication tests to be conducted in the various training areas in Belize. Therefore, the HF Test Team (HFTT), consisting of eight personnel, successfully tested and mapped the HF communications over a period of fourteen days. The goal was to ensure that tactical and safety communications could be maintained throughout at least JW(I)C 2017 by thoroughly testing HF communications both day and night. With the necessary improvements and solutions implemented, the creation of a Standard Operations Procedure (SOP) for "communications in a jungle environment" is currently in progress. NORTHERN COASTS (September 4 to October 20) The Northern Coasts deployment had multiple objectives, such as enhancing the participating units, participating in the Northern Coasts exercise, Joint Warrior 2017-2, and participation in Formidable Shield. Task Group 428.05, led by COMNL-MARFOR, consisted of the flagship Zr.Ms. Tromp, Zr.Ms. De Ruyter, Zr.Ms. Van Amstel, Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman, and BNS Louise-Marie. The MCM task group included Zr.Ms. Luymes, Zr.Ms. Schiedam, Zr.Ms. Willemstad, and BNS Narcis. During the transit to Karlskrona, a Jungle training took place in Belize.

Sea Training Command: Shore In 2017, five larger naval units began their operational training trajectory. For the smaller units, including tugs, training, diving, and landing craft, the transition to the PvB system has commenced. This involves separating the training of the crew from the platform. Ten of these smaller platforms have been delivered as operationally ready, and twenty personnel have obtained their PvB certification. Even during the operational period of the units, they are monitored and corrected where necessary. Five so-called CTs have been conducted, part of which took place in the West. For four units, it was determined after inspection that the operations were sufficiently in order to commence scheduled maintenance and then resume the training trajectory. In the first month of the year, the training trajectory of Zr.Ms. Evertsen was completed through a Staff Sea Check and a SARC 4. The Operations Directorate completed the SARC-4 for Zr.Ms. Evertsen, which was declared exercise-ready by C-STC. Shortly thereafter, STC provided support for a limited CT trajectory of Zr.Ms. Van Amstel as a supplement to the regular PDT planned before departure to the West. 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-12 87 Operations Directorate From May 8 to 16, Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman was the next ship to undergo maintenance by STC. Due to circumstances, this was the 3rd SARC-3 for the ship in the past four years. The warship had previously been deployed early for an extraordinary mission and had to deal with a serious propulsion problem, which meant it could never fully complete its regular training trajectory. This SARC-3 was taken up after a long repair period of both Main Electric Motors (HEM). The ship was trained in basic safety procedures and damage control. After completing the SARC-3, the sailing readiness status was confirmed again. May also saw STC-GBW focused on the training of Zr.Ms. Van Speyk. Together with her partner ship Zr.Ms. De Ruyter, both vessels departed on May 27 towards the south of Great Britain to the South Coast Exercise Areas for a SARC-4 program. This exercise area was chosen again because a balanced and specific training program can be developed there for warships in cooperation with FOST. Since Zr.Ms. Van Speyk was equipped with the Low Frequency Active and Passive Sonar (LFAPS) sonar system, a specific training program was developed with an emphasis on anti-submarine warfare. Unfortunately, since the involved submarine was withdrawn early, STC largely reverted to the standard trajectory. Over the weekend, both ships paid a port visit to Portsmouth. After two intensive training weeks, both ships, with an opposed entry, returned to the port of Den Helder on June 2. During an All Hands, C-STC informed the crew that the ship was training-ready and could continue its training trajectory. After successfully completing SARC 5 & 6 with FOST, Zr.Ms. Van Speyk was declared operationally ready and, on her departure to the West, underwent a PDT after which she was also mission-specific ready for her role as SSCG. On June 11, STC-GBW, again with support from the SCBRNDCBV school (OPOE team), KMTO, and DMI, departed from Zeebrugge for a PDT of BNS Louise-Marie. The ship received training in preparation for her mission in the Mediterranean Sea, Operation Sophia. This mission aims to combat human smuggling and arms trafficking in the eastern part of the Mediterranean Sea. Up to Malaga, the PDT focused on fire and damage control, after which the training became more mission-specific. After a staff change in Malaga, the ship set course towards the east of Sicily to conduct a boarding exercise with the Italian Navy. Along the way, exercises were conducted in intercepting refugees, deploying the Fire Support Team, handling prisoners, and training the boarding team. The crew also practiced flight operations with the deployed...

On June 18, the mobile team was deployed to Tallinn to conduct a NATO test with the Sakala. During those training sessions, the Swedish naval commander Rear Admiral Jens Nykvist paid a two-day working visit to MOST. Maritime Headquarters ABNL 
The Maritime Headquarters ABNL (MHK ABNL) is part of the Operations Directorate of the CZSK. The MHK is responsible for Belgian and Dutch operations and exercises of fleet and marine units. The MHK ABNL: Programs, plans, directs, coordinates, and supports operational readiness activities. Prepares mandated operations, executes them, and supports these operations. Prepares operations on behalf of the CDS and supports them. Provides general advice on maritime military operations. Drafts the bi-national operational year plan (OJP) and oversees the realization of the assigned activities. Additionally, the MHK ABNL serves as the 24/7 point of contact and coordination within CZSK for operational matters.

The Operations Directorate faced challenges with Zr.Ms. Friesland and Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt. Both units were plagued by material shortcomings, resulting in a difficult start. However, through combined efforts, the SARC-3 for both units was concluded with a satisfactory result. Both vessels were therefore declared ready for sailing in a timely manner. The year was to be concluded with two training periods, the CT for Zr.Ms. Holland and the SARC-4 for Zr.Ms. Friesland. Due to class-wide issues with the water mist installation of the patrol vessel, both ships were unable to complete their training trajectory. Support for the ACT(ASW) of Zr.Ms. Van Amstel also could not proceed due to technical problems. 

Sea Training Command: MOST 

MOST provided training for 27 units from eight different countries during 58 sailing weeks in 2017. The mobile MOST team was deployed four times in four different countries in 2017. The year began with the CT for BNS Primula, while the Sea Acceptance Trials (SATs) and the SARC 3 for Zr.Ms. Makkum were conducted simultaneously. In early February, MOST provided support to Standing NATO Mine Countermeasures Group 1 (SNMCMG) while it was in Zeebrugge. During this execution, two Italian seariders from La Spezia were guests at MOST as observers. At the end of February, a CT for BNS Godetia was conducted, and training was provided for Willemstad. Subsequently, CTs for Zr.Ms. Snellius, Zr.Ms. Vlaardingen, and BNS Lobelia were conducted. The mobile team underwent an extended Fast Cruise (FC) of Zr.Ms. Mercuur in week 13 in Den Helder. An extended FC was necessary because the Varende Materieels Beproevingen (VMBs) commenced immediately after extensive maintenance and significant propulsion modifications. 

At the beginning of spring, the SARC 3 and 4 for Zr.Ms. Luymes were scheduled, while the other team conducted the CT for BNS Narcis. Immediately after, the FC and VMBs for Zr.Ms. Urk were on the agenda. In May, a NATO test of the Latvian ship Virsaitis was planned; for its execution, a mobile team flew to Liepaja, Latvia. At the same time, the other team was deployed in Zeebrugge for the execution of the SARC-3 of Zr.Ms. Mercuur, followed by the SARC-3 of Zr.Ms. Urk and the VMBs of BNS Bellis. On June 6, the German minehunter Sulzbach Rosenberg was present in Zeebrugge for a NATO test. The other training team conducted a CT for BNS Castor and BNS Bellis.

Directie Operaties embarked Allouette III. On June 20, the staff debarked in Augusta, after which the ship was ready for its mission. After the summer leave, the staff embarked on board Zr.Ms. Rotterdam to also conduct a PDT with this ship. This training was carried out during the outbound journey to the Anti-Piracy mission Atalanta. For this, several enablers were embarked, including a Cougar helicopter from the 300 Squadron DHC, a Swedish Enhanced Boarding Element (EBE), an EBE from the Corps of Marines, a Swedish CB90 squadron, three FRISC’s from SATG, and an ART. Since all these modules needed to be prepared for the mission, a diverse staff was assembled consisting of personnel from KMTO, DMI, the SCBRNDCBV school, MTC, Defence Intelligence and Security Institute (DIVI), Defence Helicopter Command (DHC), and MHKC. The first part of the PDT focused on fire, damage control, and the individual preparation of the enablers. After the staff change in Malaga, the focus shifted to the mission and the integration of the enablers. A transit to Malta followed, where a two-day exercise program took place with the Maltese Defence Force. After part of the staff was dropped off in La Valetta, Malta, the ship continued its journey towards Crete to conduct two large boarding exercises at the NATO Maritime Interdiction Operations Training Centre (NMIOTC). After this, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam was ready for its mission and continued its journey towards Port Said. While part of the staff conducted the PDT on Zr.Ms. Rotterdam, another part of the staff embarked on Sunday, September 3, on board Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman to commence SARC-4. After Karel Doorman departed from Rotterdam, a rendezvous was made with units of the Dutch task group, which was under the command of MBS NLMARFOR. Together, they practiced seamanship and navigation skills. The Belgian NH90 helicopter embarked on board practiced with the Dutch ships and conducted dual spot operations with a Dutch NH90 from Zr.Ms. Van Amstel on board Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman. The entire squadron set course for the Swedish Karlskrona for the Pre SAIL conference of the Northern Coasts exercise. In Karlskrona, the rest of the STC staff, who had previously supported the PDT of Zr.Ms. Rotterdam, boarded. With a complete staff, the ship departed on Monday, September 11, along with all other units, for the Northern Coasts exercise at sea. After two days of intensive training, the ship was recalled to the Netherlands to take on supplies and provide support to the Windward Islands, which had been affected by Hurricane Irma. Due to this change of mission, the ship could not complete its SARC-4. The last two deployments of the year 2017 were twice a SARC-3 of respect.

Directie Operaties From June 29 to July 7, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam departed to sea for helicopter trials (Vlicozee), the Practical Training for Officer of the Marines (POTOM), and the Helicopter Qualification Week. From July 10 to July 17, the exercise CERTIFEX was conducted for the training of the 13 Raiding Squadron. The summer leave followed in week 30 through week 32. Immediately after, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam prepared for departure to the Somali basin for the anti-piracy mission EUNAVFOR Somalia. On Sunday, August 27, the ship set sail with its crew. The permanent crew of Zr.Ms. Rotterdam was supplemented with a Role 2, 300 squadron, marines with an amphibious team and a boarding team, a Swedish detachment with an amphibious team and a boarding team of Swedish marines, a sniper, intelligence personnel, and interpreters. In addition to the personnel reinforcement, extra equipment was present, including a Cougar, FRISCs, and two Swedish CB-90s. The first two weeks were focused on pre-deployment training under the leadership of STC. Subsequently, the ship was deemed operationally ready by C-STC after which they disembarked in Crete. After passing through the Suez Canal, the mission officially commenced under the leadership of an Italian staff. From September 30 to October 28, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam was off the coast of Somalia.

5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-17 92 Directorate Operations Operational Units Fleet Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt Commander: Captain (ktz) W.L. van Zanten In the summer of 2017, Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt came out of Designated Maintenance and the crew was placed on board. 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-19 94 The Operations Directorate was tasked with executing operation AEOLUS. This operation was aimed at gathering intelligence to be used for a key leader engagement. The first phase took place off the northern coast of Somaliland/Puntland and then proceeded south along the coast of Somalia. Just before the first port visit in the Seychelles, Neptunus and Neptunia boarded to 'baptize' the 'waves' while crossing the equator. Subsequently, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam anchored off Port Victoria. The second part of the mission was also focused on operation AEOLUS. After that, the port of Mombasa was visited where the local authorities hosted a reception. On Saturday, October 14, two bomb attacks occurred in Mogadishu resulting in over 800 dead and injured. Zr.Ms. Rotterdam was asked to investigate whether medical support was possible. Discussions were held at Mogadishu International Airport with representatives from local hospitals. Zr.Ms. Rotterdam then provided the necessary aid supplies. From November 1 to 5, Salalah, Oman, was visited for resupply and rest and recreation for the crew. The transit from Salalah to Djibouti was focused on conducting friendly approaches. On November 13, the mission officially came to an end. In Djibouti, VPD packages were loaded for transport to the Netherlands. The journey continued through the Suez Canal to Lisbon, where the ship arrived on November 26. On November 29, the journey continued to the home port of Den Helder, where Zr.Ms. Rotterdam arrived on Sunday, December 3. After a short disembarkation leave, the ship prepared for the scheduled maintenance period and a sustainment program following the winter leave. Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman Commander: Captain (ktz) S.L. Schot At the beginning of 2017, Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman was still docked in Den Helder, waiting for the reinstallation of the starboard HEM. The port side HEM had been reinstalled at the end of 2016 due to a defect. In January, the ship hosted the traditional New Year's run and dive of the entire Nieuwe Haven. Later that month, a detachment formed an honor guard during the visit of the Chief of Defence of New Zealand to The Hague. The ship was also visited as part of the working visit by the European faction of the CDA and by a delegation from the Indonesian navy.

Directorate Operations organized a maritime day for CZSK. Approximately 600 guests witnessed the operational capabilities during a demonstration of oil loading with Zr.Ms. Holland. In Rotterdam itself, the ship supported the opening reception of the World Port Days with several prominent visitors and a Reservists Employers Day. Onboard, the promotion of Prince Maurits to Captain (ktz) of the Royal Netherlands Navy Reserve took place. Additionally, the ship was open to the public and received over 12,000 visitors onboard. After these busy days, the ship set sail again to participate in the Northern Coasts exercise in the Baltic Sea. At the same time, the vessel was prepared under the guidance of STC. What was planned as a five-week voyage with a large Dutch squadron turned out differently when the ship received orders to return to Den Helder. Due to the hurricane season and the damage caused by Hurricane Irma on the island of Sint Maarten and other Windward Islands, the ship immediately joined Zr.Ms. Zeeland and Zr.Ms. Pelikaan to provide emergency assistance in the West. The ship arrived on September 15 in Den Helder, loading Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman with aid supplies for Sint Maarten.

5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-20 95 Operations Directorate At the beginning of February, the first "warm" test was conducted on the port HEM; the Harbour Acceptance Test (HAT). This day coincided with SARC 1. The ship also hosted the TECH information day and received a visit from a delegation of the Karel Doorman Fund Foundation. On February 17, the starboard HEM arrived in Den Helder, after which the process of reinstallation began immediately. On February 27, a crew detachment was present in The Hague during the commemoration of the Battle of the Java Sea, and during a similar commemoration at Museum Bronbeek in Arnhem. The commander, Captain (ktz) S.L. Schot, was also present at a commemoration of the Battle of the Java Sea later that week at the Karel Doorman monument at the Dutch war cemetery Kembang Kuning in Surabaya, Indonesia. The training program continued with the Slow Cruise and the FT on April 19, after which the ship set sail on April 20 for the first time since both HEMs were reinstalled, to conduct SAT. It was a positive boost for the enthusiastic crew that everything was functioning properly again. Subsequently, under the leadership of STC, SARC-3 was conducted, during which the ship made a brief port visit to Southampton. At the beginning of May, a crew delegation attended a memorial service at the National War Cemetery in Loenen. During this period, the ship received a visit from the Association of Former Officers of the Technical and Electrical Service. It then departed again to sea to conduct maritime equipment trials. At the beginning of June, the ship sailed towards Norway to perform some tests near Bergen. After conducting these tests, Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman made a brief port visit to Haakonsvern, after which it returned to Den Helder for the next event; the Marine Days. It was the first time the ship was open to the public during the Marine Days. The event coincided with SAIL, and the ship also hosted the Captain's Dinner. During these days, over 20,600 visitors were welcomed on board. After the Marine Days, the next guests were already on the quay, as the ship, in the context of a previously signed Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with Germany, served as the base for a three-week anti-terror exercise by German Special Forces. The Germans brought along a civil target ship and two types of helicopters to Den Helder; the Sikorsky Sea King and a Sikorsky CH53. The ship was at the World Port Days in Rotterdam during the last weekend of August. It was the second time for the ship, and this time it was also prominently located at the Holland Amerikakade. Before arriving in Rotterdam, Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman conducted the re-

operations. Following this, the ship participated in the multinational exercise Baltic Operations 17 (BALTOPS 17) from 1 to 16 June in the Baltic Sea. During this exercise, Zr.Ms. De Ruyter worked closely with NATO allies and partners, enhancing interoperability and joint operational capabilities. After returning to Den Helder on 19 June, the ship underwent maintenance and crew training until the end of July. 

On 1 August, Zr.Ms. De Ruyter set sail again, this time for a deployment to the Caribbean as part of the Dutch Caribbean Coast Guard efforts. The ship conducted various patrols and provided support during the hurricane season, including humanitarian assistance and disaster relief operations. 

On 30 September, Zr.Ms. De Ruyter returned to Den Helder, where the crew was welcomed back by family and friends. The year concluded with a series of internal evaluations and preparations for the upcoming year, ensuring that the ship and crew were ready for future missions and challenges.

Operations Directorate Helder, after which efforts were made with all hands to be able to depart on Wednesday, September 20. The Karel Doorman departed towards Portsmouth to pick up several containers of emergency aid destined for the British Virgin Islands. After that, it began the crossing towards the West, where it docked in the port of Philipsburg, Sint Maarten at the beginning of October. The offloading of the aid supplies was received with great interest from Prime Minister W. Marlin, Governor E.B. Holiday, CZMCARIB Brigadier General of Marines P.J. de Vin, and other local government officials, citizens, and press. The offloading of the brought goods went smoothly; the entire ship was unloaded within 24 hours. Various dignitaries were received, such as the Commissioner of Sint Eustatius J. Woodley and the outgoing Minister of the Interior and Kingdom Relations R.H.A. Plasterk. Several crew members were deployed locally under the leadership of the Royal Netherlands Army to clear debris. The ship conducted a Replenishment In Port (RIP) with the British RFA Mounts Bay. In addition to fuel, the brought aid supplies for the British Virgin Islands were transferred. After the first offload, the ship departed again to sea to steam towards Dominica, the island that had suffered extensive damage from Hurricane Maria. A team of technical personnel remained in Sint Maarten to assist the army with operations. After delivering water for the population in Dominica, the ship embarked aid supplies in nearby Guadeloupe. After dropping off these goods in Dominica, the Karel Doorman returned to Sint Maarten, after which it set course towards the ABC islands. In Curaçao and Aruba, goods were loaded for Sint Maarten, and via the Dominican Republic, where food from the World Food Programme was taken on board for Dominica, the vessel again set course for Sint Maarten and Dominica. In Sint Maarten, aid supplies were unloaded again, and a RIP was conducted with Zr.Ms. Zeeland. Additionally, children from the local Oranjeschool were given a tour of the ship. After departing from Sint Maarten, the ship set course for Martinique to pick up emergency aid for Dominica. On the latter island, emergency aid was unloaded again. To make room at the quay, the ship quickly departed again to sea. Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman carried out the redeployment for the entire task force present in Sint Maarten. The onload was a significant task for which a new loading plan was developed.

5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-25 100 Operations Directorate Zr.Ms. De Zeven Provinciën Commander: Lt. Commander (kltz) E.C.W. Jansen In 2017, Zr.Ms. De Zeven Provinciën was undergoing multi-year maintenance. Zr.Ms. Evertsen Commander: Lt. Commander (kltz) W.H. van Gemeren The year 2017 started off intensively for Zr.Ms. Evertsen: After a stormy Staff Sea Check, the ship and her crew were prepared from January 16 to 27 as part of the SARC4 for the upcoming Netherlands Operational Sea Training (NOST) period. On February 11, Zr.Ms. Evertsen entered the port of Plymouth and commenced the NOST. It was a very educational period in which the crew of Zr.Ms. Evertsen was elevated to a higher level in all aspects. Zr.Ms. Van Speijk Commander: kltz R. van Twuijver With a crew of 160, the new station ship Zr.Ms. Van Speijk entered the Annabaai of Curaçao for the first time on November 10. Unlike its predecessor, this period a multipurpose frigate carries out the tasks of the station ship. Its arrival was accompanied by the usual ceremonial events, saluting shots, and honors to the Governor of Curaçao. The first port visit of Zr.Ms. Van Speijk to Aruba also included such ceremonies. Together with the coast guard, the ship rescued nine castaways. The DASH-8 patrol aircraft from the Caribbean Coast Guard discovered the distressed vessel. Zr.Ms. Van Speijk was nearby when the crew of the ship indicated that it was taking on water and sinking. Shortly thereafter, a fire broke out, and it was reported over the radio that the ship was unmanageable. The nine crew members (6 Venezuelans, 2 Colombians, and 1 Dominican) then jumped overboard. With the NH90 onboard helicopter and the small vessels from Van Speijk, the castaways were retrieved from the water, taken aboard Zr.Ms. Van Speijk, and provided with care. Furthermore, the operations of Zr.Ms. Van Speijk included various patrols and exercises in the Caribbean region. The ship conducted maritime security operations and participated in joint exercises with local authorities. The crew also engaged in community outreach activities, strengthening ties with the local population.

Zr.Ms. Zeeland Commander: Lt. Commander (kltz) A. van der Kamp Zr.Ms. Zeeland departed from the port of Den Helder during the Marine Days to make the crossing to the Caribbean. During the outbound journey, a fire broke out on the port side HVD. Due to prompt action with handheld fire extinguishers, the damage was limited, and the journey could continue with a functioning HVD. During the crossing, the ship's boarding team was trained by the Boarding Operations Bureau. Due to excessive fuel consumption, the ship had to make an unscheduled port visit to Ponta Delgada in Madeira. During the crossing, the second HVD failed, causing the ship to make the crossing using only two patrol electric motors (PEM) at a maximum speed of 8 knots. After 13 days on the PEMs, Zr.Ms. Zeeland and her crew reached Curaçao on July 12. On September 4, Zr.Ms. Zeeland received the order to provide emergency assistance following the passage of Hurricane Irma. The ship sailed via Aruba, where emergency relief supplies and personnel were taken on board. The exercise of the abandonment role of Zr.Ms. Zeeland in Den Helder via a liferaft.

At the end of September, Zr.Ms. Groningen was cold-moved to the Rijkswerf, where maintenance began. From November 24, the ship was in the dock at the Rijkswerf. Zr.Ms. Holland Commander: kltz P.C.B. Dijkhuizen EMSD The deployment of Zr.Ms. Holland this year consisted of three parts: a training program led by C-STC, Coast Guard duties, and counter-drug operations. After the maintenance period in Curaçao, Zr.Ms. Holland conducted CD operations from December 13, 2016, to January 20, 2017, with support from the USCG LEDET and a Guard Aviation Detachment with an MH-65 Dolphin helicopter. After completing a joint training/integration period, the ship was ready for Operation Carib Venture under the leadership of CTG 4.4. During this period, two drug transports were disrupted, and the ship was closely involved in a controlled overload of contraband. On the last patrol day, the ship intercepted a suspicious vessel that was landing on Bonaire with narcotics, a firearm, and two individuals. Zr.Ms. Holland also assisted a British sailing yacht that was experiencing hydraulic problems with its steering system. The technical personnel of Zr.Ms. Holland repaired the installation, allowing the sailing yacht to continue its journey to Bonaire under its own power.

5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-40 115 The Operations Directorate embarked and sailed to the Windward Islands of the Kingdom. Zr.Ms. Zeeland provided support to the Commander of the 'emergency aid' detachment, later renamed Commander Joint Task Force Sint-Maarten. The priorities were to support security and transport tasks, assess the damage, and operationalize the infrastructure (including the air and seaport). Four days after Hurricane Irma passed, a second hurricane announced itself in the region: José. As a result, both Zr.Ms. Zeeland and Zr.Ms. Pelikaan (which was also in Sint-Maarten for emergency aid) had to leave the port to seek shelter at a safe distance. Fortunately, the damage from Hurricane José was limited. On September 19, a third hurricane approached: Maria. After tearing across Dominica, Maria veered towards Puerto Rico, sparing the Dutch Windward Islands from further disaster. As the emergency aid in Sint-Maarten transitioned to a reconstruction phase, Zr.Ms. Zeeland, Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman, and Zr.Ms. Pelikaan provided emergency aid to Dominica. Distributing essential supplies to isolated areas and conducting medical evacuations were the tasks of these naval vessels. In total, Zeeland and her crew operated for 36 consecutive days at sea and on land as part of emergency aid operations. Due to the emergency aid operations, Zr.Ms. Zeeland could be deployed more restrictively for coast guard tasks. Nevertheless, the ship managed to rescue a 60-year-old sailor from Saint Vincent from the water during her coast guard periods and participated in Operation Lockdown Aruba. On the first night of Zr.Ms. Zeeland's return journey, the Coast Guard's DASH-8 aircraft spotted a suspicious boat. Both the NH90 helicopter and the two FRISC boats were deployed to intercept the vessel. After it ignored warning shots, disabling fire was used to disable the outboard motors. The occupants of the boat threw suspicious packages overboard. With the FRISC, 348 kilograms of cocaine were retrieved from the water. Minehunter Zr.Ms. Makkum Commander: Lt. Cdr. B.R.P. Very High Readiness Joint Task Force (Land) (VJTF(L)) The VJTF(L) is a rapidly deployable brigade and is under British command. 13 RSQN completed its training cycle in the first half of 2017. The squadron consisted of a staff and two Troops (due to underfilling during formation in 2016). Training during this period included winter training in Norway, SOUT training in Germany, Basic Helicopter Training, and fast rope training in the Netherlands, culminating in Maritime Interdiction Operations (MIO) training and MARSOC certification exercise. With the completion of the training cycle, 13 RSQN was certified MARC-4 in July 2017. In the second half of 2017, 13 RSQN conducted the Black Horse exercise at the US Marine Corps Air Ground Combat Center in Twentynine Palms (Mojave Desert, California). The objective of this exercise was to conduct tactical shooting exercises up to squadron level. In the autumn, 13 RSQN carried out, among other things, the military tracker course in Aruba. For the CBMI mission, 13 RSQN assembled and trained a training team to be deployed in Iraq in January 2018. 14 CS SQN consists of three Troops: Anti Armour (AA) Troop, Armoured All Terrain Vehicle (AATV) Troop, and Assault Engineers (AE) Troop. Throughout 2017, these Troops followed their own training programs. AE and AATV supported, with each a section, the training year of a RSQN. As a result, they participated in several exercises of the training system, such as the mobility week and the certification exercise. AE also conducted cold weather training for Marines in Norway.

5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-52 127 Operations Directorate Training and Exercises The larger exercises of 2017 included the JAT in the vicinity of Harstad (Norway), the Black Horse shooting training at Twentynine Palms (United States), and the mountain training in Garelochhead (United Kingdom). 10 CSS SQN was on 48 hours notice to move for the VJTF in 2017 with approximately half of the squadron, personnel as well as equipment. The squadron had logistical resources ready for 30 days to enable an expeditionary operation, entirely independently. At the same time, the squadron supported the other exercises of 1 MCG, in support of the MTC and also 2 MCG. Despite a significant shortage of trained personnel and the absence of many mid-level staff, all assignments were able to proceed. When activating emergency aid to the Windward Islands following Hurricane Irma, 10 CSS SQN, partly due to the preparation for VJTF, was able to prepare and push out all necessary materials and supporting personnel within 24 hours via Eindhoven Airport and the port of Den Helder. 11 RSQN underwent parachute training in the first half of 2017 and supported 2 MCG with the Eagle Niala exercise. In the context of preparation for the VJTF(L), 11 RSQN participated in the ALERT EX in the Netherlands and the DEPLOY EX in Romania. After the summer leave, 11 RSQN was deployed as MSTU for emergency aid to the Windward Islands following the passage of Hurricane Irma. Shortly after the emergency aid, novices from the unit were able to participate in the mountain training. At the end of 2017, 11 RSQN prepared to provide 5 VPD teams starting January 1, 2018. Throughout the year, 11 RSQN was on standby in the context of the VJTF and the MSTU. 12 RSQN carried out various smaller activities in the first half of 2017 such as VPD deployment, boarding training in the Nieuwe Haven, Hunter Force, participation in the Cutlass Express exercise in Djibouti/Mauritius, support for training and exercises, and various ceremonial tasks including the Normandy commemoration. Furthermore, 12 RSQN phased out in the first half of 2017 to start with a newly formed crew in August 2018 for the preparation year. Due to insufficient outflow from the EMV, 12 RSQN began the preparation year with only two Troops instead of three. From August to October, functional training for the various specialists within the squadron, such as infantry engineers (IE), marksmen, and section commanders, was the focus. Subsequently, the unit conducted shooting training in Otterburn, United Kingdom.

5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-60 135 Operations Directorate Training and Exercises At the beginning of the year, the unit was not yet certified. Therefore, all training was focused on preparing and being ready for the certification moment in July. For the LCTU, the first joint training was a unit training at the Stuifdijk on Texel, where the Amphibious Beach Unit (ABU) was deployed and the vessels operated according to a Surface Assault (SURFALT) to and from the beach. At the end of February, the unit departed for ISHK to maintain individual skills and drills on various weapon systems. In March, the CERTIFEX for the 22nd RSQN took place. LCTU-2 had to support this training, which was also a good dress rehearsal for its own certification in July. The first part of the exercise took place in the vicinity of Vlissingen, using the Marine barracks as a Forward Operating Base (FOB). The second part of the exercise was at the Kop van Noord-Holland, where we operated from Zr.Ms. Rotterdam. After the CERTIFEX, LCTU-2 conducted some of its own training sessions. Additionally, LCTU-2 repeated several annual activities in May and June, including the Military Basic Skills (MBV) and the FPM. LCTU-2 provided the amphibious demonstrations at the end of June during the Marine Days and SAIL Den Helder. Furthermore, the unit was responsible for coordination on the water. After the Landing Craft Task Element (LCTE) went on mission with Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman, there was not much left of the LCTU, and the ABU recce conducted a reconnaissance in Norway. 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-61 136 Operations Directorate Operational Deployment At the beginning of the year, it became known that not the entire LCTU would accompany Zr.Ms. Rotterdam for the Atalanta mission off the Horn of Africa. The only components of LCTU-2 were the FRISC section and two communicators. From the moment this was announced, the FRISC section worked as closely as possible with Zr.Ms. Rotterdam to actually depart towards Somalia after the summer leave. During this mission, they conducted various patrols in cooperation with Swedish colleagues. On September 6, Hurricane Irma passed over the Leeward Islands, severely impacting Sint Maarten, Sint Eustatius, and Saba. Despite the presence of units on the islands, the devastation was so great that there was a need for additional personnel and equipment. For LCTU-2, this meant that the commander of the unit was flown in to assist and participate in the staff of the rotating elements, the 32nd and the 11th RSQN on the island. This support at the staff level lasted three weeks. Two weeks after Hurricane Irma, the decision was made to also send Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman to the Caribbean to provide humanitarian assistance. This decision was influenced by the fact that the now-passed Hurricane Maria had caused significant damage in Dominica. In addition to transporting many goods with Karel Doorman, an LCTE from LCTU-2 was also attached to the ship. This element included two Landing Craft Vehicle and Personnel (LCVPs) and a small staff. The LCTE carried out support by conducting various patrols in cooperation with the Coast Guard on Sint Maarten. A marine receives a compliment during the distribution of water on Sint Maarten.
